findings.claim: Diversified, slow (1-12 month) time-series momentum / trend following is the only family here with long, multi-source, cost-inclusive evidence - but its performance decayed sharply after 2009 (roughly when it was popularised), and it is cyclical with deep multi-year drawdowns.
findings.evidence: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (JPM 2017, read in full text): 67 markets, 1880-2016, 'positive average returns in each market, with an average Sharpe ratio of approximately 0.4' gross per market; secondary summaries report a diversified net Sharpe of about 0.76 after simulated costs and 2/20 fees. Goulding, Harvey & Mazzoleni (FAJ 2024, Table E.1 read directly; 43 futures incl. 24 commodities): static 12-month trend Sharpe 1.07 in 1990-2008 vs 0.06 in 2009-2022 (full sample 0.64); 1-month trend 0.61 vs 0.01. Their footnote: SG Trend Index Sharpe about 0.41 in 2000-2009 vs 0.21 in 2010-2019. They and AQR (Babu et al. 2020) attribute the decay to more turning points / fewer large moves, not proven crowding - that attribution is interpretation, not fact. Cambridge Associates: SG Trend fell 20.4% May 2024-May 2025 (second-largest drawdown since 2000) after +27.4% in 2022. 2025 finished about +2.4% (secondary source). These are multi-asset results, not gold-specific.

findings.claim: On a single instrument (gold or silver alone) trend following is NOT a statistically established edge; most of the published 'alpha' comes from diversification across dozens of markets and from volatility scaling.
findings.evidence: Huang, Li, Wang & Zhou (JFE 2020), re-using the Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen data: asset-by-asset regressions show little evidence of time-series momentum in or out of sample; the pooled t-statistic falls below bootstrap critical values; a TSM strategy performs virtually the same as one based on the historical mean sign. Kim, Tse & Wald (J. Financial Markets 2016): without volatility scaling, TSMOM and buy-and-hold have similar cumulative returns and alphas not significantly different. Hurst et al.: per-market gross Sharpe averages only about 0.4 over 136 years. Inference: a two-instrument, highly correlated gold/silver book should expect a Sharpe well below the diversified figures and multi-year flat or losing stretches. I could not retrieve verified per-instrument gold/silver TSMOM Sharpe ratios from the original 2012 paper (host unavailable); a secondary replication claiming about 0.4 for gold and a Quantopian replication showing slightly negative values are both unverified.

findings.claim: Transaction-cost sensitivity splits the families cleanly: slow trend is almost cost-immune in futures terms, while every documented intraday gold effect has a gross edge of only a few basis points per trade - the same order as round-trip costs.
findings.evidence: Confirmed inputs: Goulding et al. Table E.1 gives annual turnover of 229% for 12-month trend and 1,135% for 1-month trend; Harvey et al. (JPM 2018) use 1.0 bp of notional per trade as the institutional cost estimate for gold futures. Inference (my arithmetic): trend costs about 2-11 bp per year, negligible. By contrast the Baltussen et al. commodity intraday-momentum portfolio earns 4.34% a year gross on daily trades, about 1.7 bp per trade, versus about 2 bp round trip at 1 bp per side; GLD overnight holding averages about 4 bp per trade gross (commercial blog figure). Not verified here: actual retail CFD spread in bp at today's gold price, commissions, slippage and overnight swap; for multi-week CFD holds the financing/swap charge, not the spread, is likely the dominant cost and could materially reduce slow-trend returns.

findings.claim: Classic technical trading rules (moving-average crossovers, channel breakouts, etc.) on commodities and intraday gold/silver mostly fail once data snooping is controlled; silver is worse than gold.
findings.evidence: Marshall, Cahan & Cahan (J. Banking & Finance 2008): 7,846 rules, 15 commodity futures, 1984-2005; after data-snooping adjustment no reliable profits in 14 of 15 (oats only, and that vanished in 1995-2005). Batten, Lucey, McGroarty, Peat & Urquhart (JIFMIM 2018; 5-minute spot data Jan 2008-Sep 2014, 66,297 MA parameter combinations): standard parameters have 'no predictive power whatsoever' / negative payoffs; only long-window rules show some predictability in gold (per the working-paper summary, 20.2% of SMA, 1.3% of EMA and 1.9% of WMA rules significantly positive) and none in silver; results are gross of transaction costs, so net results are worse. Charles, Darne & Kim (IRFA 2015): return predictability of gold and silver has trended downward; gold 'highly efficient recently'.

findings.claim: Intraday momentum (rest-of-day return predicting the last 30 minutes) is statistically real in gold and stronger in silver, but economically tiny, measured gross of costs, and tied to a session definition that no longer matches the 23-hour electronic market.
findings.evidence: Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (JFE 2021), Table B3 read directly: COMEX gold 1984-2020, slope 1.09 (x100), t = 2.95, in-sample R2 0.25%, out-of-sample R2 0.08%; silver slope 2.93, t = 5.44, R2 1.42%, OOS R2 1.01%. Sessions used are legacy pit hours (gold 08:20-13:30 ET). Commodity-class strategy: 4.34% a year, 3.05% vol, Sharpe 1.42 - gross. The authors state: 'we do not consider transaction costs... the strategy as presented might not be exploitable to many investors after accounting for transaction costs.' Chinese SHFE studies (Ma, Bouri, Xu & Zhou 2025 and related) show the predictive half-hour moved from the day session to the night session once night trading launched, i.e. the specification is not stable across market-structure changes. Net-of-cost gold results were not found.

findings.claim: Opening-range, London-session and New-York-session breakouts on gold are folklore as far as published evidence goes: I found no peer-reviewed, cost-inclusive test on gold; what exists is vendor backtests. The academic ORB evidence is on crude oil and US equities, and an independent replication on index CFDs found the edge is consumed by costs.
findings.evidence: Holmberg, Lonnbark & Lundstrom (Finance Research Letters 2013) find ORB returns significantly above zero - on crude oil futures, not gold. Zarattini, Barbon & Aziz (SSRN 2024, practitioner paper, read directly) report a 5-minute ORB on US 'stocks in play' 2016-2023 with Sharpe 2.81 net of commissions only. A vendor replication of the related QQQ ORB rule on NQ/SPX/Dow/DAX/FTSE CFDs (Jan 2015-Jun 2026) reproduced the gross +0.13R on NQ but net of spread and slippage no market was distinguishable from zero (NQ +0.002R; others -0.04R to -0.08R). The only gold London-breakout result found is an MQL5 seller's MT5 backtest (Jan 2023-Sep 2026, profit factor 1.37-1.38, max drawdown 17-19% at 1% risk, cost assumptions undisclosed, parameters tuned on the same data, and the whole sample is a strong gold bull market). What IS confirmed is time-of-day structure in volatility, volume and spread (Batten et al., PLoS ONE 2017, 5-minute data 2000-2015; spreads lowest in European hours) - sessions predict how much gold moves and how cheap it is to trade, not the direction.

findings.claim: The gold overnight / Asian-hours drift is a genuinely documented anomaly (positive returns outside Western trading hours, flat-to-negative returns during them), but it has weakened, its 'fixing-time sell-off' component was regime-specific (about 2007-2012), and it is marginal to untradable after realistic costs.
findings.evidence: Blose & Gondhalekar (Applied Economics Letters 2014): COMEX front contract 1985-2012, overnight returns significantly positive and day returns significantly negative; the asymmetry 'has weakened substantially over the years, but it is still present'. Blose, Gondhalekar & Kort (J. Economics & Finance 2018): same sign in COMEX futures, London fix, miners and funds, in up and down markets; the abstract says it remains economically important after transaction costs (effect sizes not retrieved - paywalled). Caminschi & Heaney (J. Futures Markets 2014): trades in the first minutes of the PM fix predicted the fix direction (information leakage) - pre-reform; the fix was replaced by the electronic LBMA Gold Price auction in March 2015. CBS master's thesis (COMEX tick data 2001-2018, read directly): the rising 'East' leg (17:00-03:00 ET) is the consistent part; the Western decline is not robust (positive in 8 of 18 years); fixing-time drops are stable only in 2007-2012; strategies reach Sharpe 1.61 gross but with costs do not beat buy-and-hold. Quantified Strategies (2026, commercial blog): GLD overnight about 0.04% per trade and roughly equal to buy-and-hold, intraday flat, 'probably not tradable after costs'. Quantpedia: OHLC opening prints inflate overnight backtests (GDX overnight about 30% a year on OHLC vs 8.6% when exiting at 09:31). Claims such as '64% annualized long-overnight/short-intraday' come from advocacy sites with no costs. No peer-reviewed post-2018 test was found.

findings.claim: Short-horizon mean reversion (fade the big day, RSI-style pullback buying) has no credible cost-surviving evidence on gold or silver; the limited evidence points the other way (continuation after large moves).
findings.evidence: Caporale, Gil-Alana & Plastun (CESifo WP 5066 / Computational Economics 2018), which uses a MetaTrader strategy-tester 'trading robot': a counter-movement strategy after one-day overreactions 'does not generate profits in the FOREX and the commodity markets' (gold), while an 'inertia' (continuation) strategy does - on a short 2012-2014 test window, so weak evidence either way. A review of Urquhart & Zhang reports commodity futures show momentum but not reversal (secondary). Charles et al. (2015) show gold and silver predictability trending down. Pandini's z-score reversion on the gold-silver spread lost heavily after 2020 (see pairs finding). No peer-reviewed, post-cost test of intraday or daily mean reversion specifically on spot gold/silver was found, so this is absence of evidence plus mild counter-evidence.

findings.claim: Gold-silver ratio pairs trading rests on a cointegration relationship that is unstable and regime-dependent; the mean-reversion trade has worked in windows and then failed violently, most recently in 2020 and 2025-26.
findings.evidence: Escribano & Granger (1998): cointegration only in some periods (bubble and post-bubble), weaker out of sample. Baur & Tran (2014): cointegration over 1970-2011 but shaped by bubbles and crises. Pierdzioch, Risse & Rohloff (Finance Research Letters 2015): 'a cointegration link did not exist during extended periods of time'. Schweikert (2018): constant-vector models fail; relationship is non-linear and state-dependent. Pandini (2026, SIAT practitioner paper, not peer-reviewed, read directly; train 2007-2017, test 2018-2025, entry at z = +/-2, exit at +/-1, 10 bp cost): GLD-SLV failed in-sample Engle-Granger tests; the trade made about +16.1% a year net (Sharpe 0.29) in 2018-Jan 2020, then about -60.3% a year net (Sharpe -0.60) afterwards as the spread became non-stationary. Regime illustration (press reports; figures differ by source): ratio about 105 in April 2025, compressed to about 50 at silver's late-January 2026 peak; on 30 Jan 2026 silver fell 26-31% in one session and gold about 9%.

findings.claim: Volatility targeting and ATR-based sizing are risk-control tools, not sources of edge, for gold and silver: they do not raise the Sharpe ratio in commodities but they do reduce tail risk and stabilise risk exposure.
findings.evidence: Harvey, Hoyle, Korgaonkar, Rattray, Sargaison & Van Hemert (JPM 2018, read directly; 60+ assets, daily data from 1926): Sharpe ratios rise with volatility scaling for equities and credit, but 'for other assets, such as bonds, currencies, and commodities, volatility scaling has a negligible effect on realized Sharpe ratios'; volatility targeting 'consistently reduces the likelihood of extreme returns (and the volatility of volatility)' across assets. Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (JFE 2020; 103 equity strategies): volatility-managed portfolios do not systematically beat unmanaged ones out of sample. Kim, Tse & Wald (2016): much of TSMOM's apparent alpha is the volatility scaling itself. I found no academic study isolating ATR stops or ATR sizing on gold; claims that ATR stops add edge are untested folklore.

findings.claim: Grid, martingale and averaging-down systems have no edge of their own and a documented path to ruin: they trade a high win rate for a rare account-sized loss, and leverage is the mechanism.
findings.evidence: Taranto & Khan (Investment Management and Financial Innovations 17(3), 2020), the main academic treatment of bi-directional grid trading: such strategies can outperform other algorithms in the short term but 'will almost surely ruin an investment account in the long term' (abstract as returned by search; full-text theorem conditions not retrieved - the publisher returned 503). Standard gambler's-ruin / optional-stopping logic: bet sizing cannot convert a zero-or-negative expectancy per trade into a positive one with finite capital - this is mathematics, not an empirical claim. Empirical support on the leverage channel: Heimer & Simsek (JFE 2019) find the 2010 US retail FX leverage cap cut high-leverage traders' losses by 40%. Gap risk is real in these metals: silver's 26-31% one-day drop and gold's roughly 9% on 30 Jan 2026 would overwhelm typical grid spacing. MQL5 signal pages themselves flag 'averaging without closing losing trades' strategies with 74% win rates alongside 68% drawdowns (anecdotal).

findings.claim: The base rate for retail leveraged trading is that roughly 70-90% of accounts lose money, persistence does not help, and there is no evidence of learning - this is the prior any retail gold/silver bot should be judged against.
findings.evidence: ESMA product-intervention notice (2018, read directly): 'Between 74-89% of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs'; gold CFDs sit in the 5% initial-margin bucket (20:1). FCA sample analysis: 82% of CFD clients lost money. ASIC: 72% lost on CFDs and 63% on margin FX in its 2017 review; 68% in FY2024 (secondary reports). CFTC (Dec 2024 release, via search summary): 50.96-74% of US retail forex accounts unprofitable per quarter. Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti (SSRN): of Brazilian futures day traders who persisted over 300 days, 97% lost money and only 1.1% earned more than minimum wage; no evidence of learning. Hayley & Marsh (JIMF 2016): retail FX traders do not learn to trade better and 'even very experienced traders consistently lose money'. SEBI (Sept 2024): about 93% of individual equity-derivatives traders lost over FY22-FY24.

findings.claim: There are no credible population-level statistics on how retail expert advisors perform over time; the nearest evidence (copy-trading studies, prop-firm data, SEBI's algo split) says followers earn no abnormal return after costs and that algorithmic profits accrue to institutions, not retail.
findings.evidence: My searches found no study covering all MQL5/Myfxbook signals including dead ones; what is published is self-selected live signals and vendor backtests (survivorship and selection bias). Dorfleitner et al. (Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance 2018) on social-trading signal providers: 'no strategy reveals a positive abnormal return after transaction costs'; simply following the highest accumulated returns 'leads to high losses'; highly active trading is negatively related to returns. SEBI (2024): 97% of FPI profits and 96% of proprietary-trader profits in equity derivatives came from 'algo entities' while individuals lost in aggregate - note SEBI's definition (at least one algo order a year, including broker auto-square-offs) overstates this; an August 2026 update reportedly shows 87.7% of individuals losing and 99% of institutional profits from algo entities (press reports, not verified against SEBI's own document). Industry prop-firm data (FPFX Tech, 300,000+ accounts, unaudited, via trade press): about 14% pass a challenge and about 7% ever receive a payout. CFTC advisory (Jan 2024): automated bots and signal services promising high or guaranteed returns are a fraud red flag.

findings.claim: Recent gold-only backtests (roughly 2015-2026) are contaminated by one of the strongest gold bull markets on record, so long-biased or breakout rules look far better than they are; headline claims from this window should be discounted unless they beat buy-and-hold and work symmetrically long and short.
findings.evidence: Gold returned roughly +56% to +64% in 2025 depending on the proxy (S&P GSCI Gold ER vs GLD). An arXiv preprint (Nov 2025, not peer-reviewed) claims an out-of-sample Sharpe of 2.88 for a long-only gold-futures trend system over 2015-2025, but on reading it: realized return is 2.62% a year at 0.91% volatility, the headline 43% CAGR is an extrapolation to a 15% vol target, a table shows Sharpe 0.937 at baseline costs contradicting the text, 64 parameter configurations were tried, and profits arise almost entirely in bull regimes. The MQL5 gold London-breakout backtest covers only 2023-2026. Quantified Strategies' GLD overnight result is essentially equal to buy-and-hold over a period in which GLD rose more than 976%. Inference: any rule that is long more often than short will show a positive backtest in this window regardless of signal quality.

implications_for_bot: If the bot needs a directional core, the only evidence-backed choice is slow trend following (blend of roughly 1-, 3- and 12-month signals) with volatility-targeted sizing. Set expectations honestly: per-instrument gross Sharpe around 0.2-0.4 at best, near-zero in 2009-2022 for static rules, and multi-year drawdowns. With only two highly correlated metals there is almost no diversification, which is where most of the published trend 'alpha' comes from.

Treat every intraday idea (opening-range, London/NY breakout, last-30-minute momentum, overnight hold) as guilty until proven net of costs. Documented gross edges are about 2-4 bp per trade; require the backtested edge to be at least 2-3x the all-in round-trip cost (spread + commission + slippage + swap) measured on the actual broker feed, and benchmark against both buy-and-hold and a random-direction entry with the same stops.

Use session/time-of-day as a cost and volatility filter, not a direction signal: the confirmed facts are that volatility, volume and spreads follow a daily pattern (spreads tightest in European hours / London-NY overlap). Trade when liquidity is best, widen or stand down around rollover and scheduled news.

The overnight/Asian-hours drift can at most justify a mild tilt (for example, not initiating shorts in Asian hours, or preferring to carry existing longs overnight). Do not build a standalone strategy on it without testing 2019-2026 tick data including swap charges; the fixing-time sell-off component should be considered dead.

Do not run gold-silver ratio mean reversion as a core strategy. If it is used at all, it needs a hard stop and a time stop, volatility-balanced legs (silver is far more volatile than gold), rolling re-estimation, and a kill switch when the spread stops reverting - the 2020 and 2025-26 episodes show the trade can lose for years.

Keep ATR / volatility-based sizing and a portfolio volatility target as mandatory risk plumbing, but do not count it as alpha. Cap leverage well below broker maximums and size for gap risk that stops cannot protect against (a ~9% gold and ~26-31% silver single-session move occurred on 30 Jan 2026).

Prohibit martingale, grid and averaging-down logic in code (no adding to losers, no lot multiplication after losses). Use fixed-fractional risk per trade, daily and weekly loss limits, and a maximum-drawdown kill switch.

Backtest hygiene matters more than strategy choice: use bid/ask tick data rather than OHLC opens, walk-forward validation, a small pre-declared parameter set with a data-snooping correction (White's Reality Check / SPA or at least a count of trials), and test windows that include gold's 2011-2015 bear market and sideways years, not just 2019-2026. Require long and short sides to be evaluated separately.

Adopt the regulatory base rate as the prior: 70-90% of retail leveraged accounts lose. Design the bot so that its default assumption is zero edge minus costs, run it on demo then minimum size with pre-registered success criteria, and treat vendor EA backtests, signal-page track records and '95% win rate' claims as marketing, not evidence.
open_questions: What are the gold-specific and silver-specific time-series momentum Sharpe ratios, pre- and post-2009, net of realistic costs? The original Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen per-instrument figures could not be retrieved (host returned 503), and the only gold numbers found are unverified secondary replications that disagree in sign.

Does the overnight / Asian-hours gold drift persist in 2019-2026 after CFD swap charges and spread? No peer-reviewed post-2018 study was found, and Blose et al. (2018) effect sizes are behind a paywall.

Does last-30-minute intraday momentum survive in today's 23-hour electronic gold market? The key study uses legacy COMEX pit hours (08:20-13:30 ET) and reports gross results only; which 'close' matters now (COMEX settlement, London PM auction, 17:00 ET rollover) is untested.

What are the actual all-in costs on the intended venue - spread in basis points at the current gold and silver price, commission, slippage around news and rollover, and long/short swap rates? Every break-even statement above depends on these, and none were verified in this research. For multi-week trend holds on CFDs, financing could dominate.

Is there any dataset of retail expert advisors or MQL5/Myfxbook signals that includes discontinued ones? Without it, survival and long-run performance rates for retail EAs remain unknown rather than merely bad.
Does the gold-silver ratio show exploitable trend (momentum) rather than mean reversion in the post-2020 regime? The literature tests reversion; ratio momentum was not found in any credible study.

Were the 2024-2026 gold and silver trends (and the January 2026 crash) net positive or negative for systematic trend followers in metals specifically? 2026 year-to-date CTA figures found were conflicting and unsourced.

Verification gaps: the full text of Taranto & Khan (grid-trading ruin theorem conditions) and of Batten et al. 2018 could not be fetched; reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org did not resolve from this session and would need to be allowed in the session's network settings to check that copy. Several regulator figures (ASIC, CFTC, SEBI 2026 update) rest on press summaries rather than the primary documents.

findings.claim: Market plumbing: COMEX gold (GC) is 100 troy oz with a $0.10 tick ($10); COMEX silver (SI) is 5,000 troy oz with a $0.005 tick ($25). Globex trades Sunday-Friday 5:00 pm-4:00 pm Chicago time with a 60-minute daily break from 4:00 pm CT, i.e. 17:00-18:00 New York, and spot/CFD feeds stop for the same hour. The LBMA Gold Price auctions start at 10:30 and 15:00 London time and the LBMA Silver Price auction at 12:00 London time, administered by ICE Benchmark Administration.
findings.evidence: CME gold fact card text (as returned by search; direct fetch of cmegroup.com returned HTTP 503): 'Sunday - Friday 5:00 p.m. - 4:00 p.m. CT with an hour break each day beginning at 4:00 p.m. CT', contract size 100 troy ounces, tick 0.10 = $10. CME silver listing: 5,000 oz, 0.005 per oz = $25. ICE methodology document lists auction start times AM 10:30, PM 15:00 (gold) and 12:00 (silver), London time. Broker pages agree on the break and show it moves in UTC with US daylight saving: IG quotes spot metals 24h except 21:00-22:00 GMT; Dukascopy break 21:00-22:00 GMT in summer and 22:00-23:00 GMT in winter; Fusion Markets break 20:59-22:00 GMT (DST) and 21:59-23:00 GMT (standard); CMC says Gold Cash closes Friday 5 pm New York. The OANDA hourly feed has no bar for the 17:00 New York hour. New in 2026: CME started 24/7 trading in 1-Ounce Gold futures on 24 July 2026 and 100-Ounce Silver futures on 11 Sept 2026 (first silver weekend: 2,387 contracts, ~$15m); whether full-size GC/SI hours changed was not stated in any source found.

findings.claim: Liquidity by session: activity is concentrated in the New York morning (08:00-11:00 New York, covering US data at 08:30, the COMEX day and the 15:00 London PM auction at 10:00 New York), with a secondary burst at the Asian open (20:00-22:00 New York). The thinnest hours are the hour before the break (16:00), the reopen (18:00-19:00) and around midnight New York. In the mid-2026 sample a distinct 'London open' surge is not visible.

Peer-reviewed work (Hauptfleisch, Putnins, Lucey 2016, 17 years of intraday data) finds New York futures play the larger role in price discovery although London spot volume is far bigger; an earlier Lucey et al. study found no clear dominant venue, so this is not uncontested.

findings.claim: Retail CFD spreads: published best-case spreads on spot gold are about $0.08-0.20 on raw/razor accounts and roughly $0.20-0.60 on standard accounts, i.e. about 0.2-1.5 basis points of price; spot silver is about $0.018-0.03, i.e. about 4-6 basis points. No broker was found that publishes an hour-by-hour table; brokers state that spreads widen outside active hours, after the daily break and in stress, and the size of that widening is only documented by unverified vendor pages.
findings.evidence: Pepperstone UK spreads page (based on data 1-31 Aug 2026, all sessions including rollover): minimum spread spot gold 0.08 (Razor), 0.19 (Standard); spot silver 0.018 (Razor), 0.023 (Standard). IG MT4 details: 'normal' spread 0.6 for spot gold and 3 for spot silver. IC Markets commodity sheet (undated): average 0.63 'pips' XAUUSD and 0.09 XAGUSD plus $7 per lot round-turn commission on Raw; the pip unit is not defined. BrokerChooser (undated): gold average 0.32 across 100+ brokers, range 0.03-1.03. VT Markets 24/7 gold symbol: from 15 points on weekdays, from 40 points at weekends. Using ~$3,900 gold and ~$49 silver, silver's spread is roughly 4-10x gold's in relative terms (own arithmetic). The gold/silver ratio is unstable: it ranged 57-105 in 2025 and 46-80 in 2026, and at about 80 now sits at its 2026 high.

implications_for_bot: Read every contract parameter from the broker at start-up and on each session (contract size, tick size and tick value, volume step, minimum stop distance, margin rate, swap long/short, triple-swap day). Do not hard-code 5,000 oz for silver or any 'pip' size: one mainstream broker sheet shows 1,000 oz, and 24/7 gold symbols are 1 oz.

Size positions and stops from current volatility, not fixed dollars or points. Calibrate to the 2026 regime (gold daily ATR about $90-100 or 2.2-2.6%; silver about $2.2-3.2 or 4.4-5.5%) and re-estimate on a rolling basis; a stop distance tuned on 2024 data is about one third of today's noise in gold and about one quarter in silver.

Use a timezone-aware schedule anchored to America/New_York (and Europe/London for the 10:30, 12:00 and 15:00 auctions), not fixed UTC or server hours; the daily break sits at 21:00-22:00 UTC in US summer time and 22:00-23:00 UTC in winter, and US/UK clock changes are out of step for a few weeks a year.

Concentrate entries where range is high relative to spread: 08:00-12:00 New York first, the Asian open (20:00-22:00 New York) second. Block new entries from about 16:00 to 19:00 New York (pre-break thinning, the 17:00-18:00 halt, the reopen), and do not leave tight stops working across the break.

Add a live spread gate: record bid-ask every tick or minute by hour, and refuse entries when the spread exceeds a multiple of its rolling median or a set fraction of the stop distance. This also builds the broker-specific spread table that no source publishes. Use a stricter gate for silver, where spread eats about three times more of the hourly range.

Run a calendar-driven event mode for payrolls, CPI and PCE (08:30 New York) and FOMC (14:00 statement, 14:30 press conference): no new entries from roughly 15 minutes before to 15-30 minutes after, reduced size or flat through the release, and stops sized for a release-hour range of about 1.5% in gold and 2-2.6% in silver. Flag 9-10 December 2026, when FOMC and CPI fall on consecutive days.

Decide weekend exposure explicitly. Either be flat before Friday 17:00 New York, or size so that a 1-2% gap in gold and a 2-4% gap in silver stays inside the risk limit and above the broker's stop-out level; stop orders fill at the reopen price, not at the stop. Do not treat a broker's 24/7 gold symbol as a hedge for the standard symbol without testing it: it is a separate instrument with its own price and wider spread.

Keep large free-margin headroom and monitor margin level continuously. Assume the broker can raise margin with little notice and apply it to open positions (silver went from 5% to 20% at one broker; exchange margins doubled within a week), and that leverage may be cut before news and weekends. Handle 'not enough money', order-size-limit and trading-suspended rejections without retry loops.

Account for financing in any strategy that holds past 17:00 New York: long gold costs roughly 5-8% a year at current rates, with a triple charge on Wednesday. An intraday or scalping strategy should be flat before rollover unless the expected edge clearly exceeds the swap plus the rollover spread.

Give silver its own parameter set rather than reusing gold's: about half the notional for the same risk (beta about 2), percentage stops about twice as wide, a lower leverage assumption (10:1 or less), smaller maximum order size, and a tighter rule on weekend and event holding. Treat simultaneous same-direction gold and silver positions as one correlated exposure (correlation 0.83-0.88), not two.

Build hard circuit breakers: a daily loss limit, a kill switch when the day's range exceeds a multiple of ATR or the spread blows out, and a pause after abnormal slippage. Stress-test against 30 January 2026 (gold about -10% and silver about -30% in one session, intraday ranges of 14% and 39%) and against a 4% silver weekend gap, and confirm whether the account has negative balance protection.

Backtest with variable spreads, swaps, the daily break and both regimes (2024 low volatility and 2026 high volatility). A result that only holds on fixed-spread data or on one regime should not be trusted for sizing.
open_questions: Which broker, legal entity and account type will the bot trade on? Contract size, pip definition, leverage cap, stop-out level, swap rates, event/weekend margin windows and negative balance protection all depend on it, and none can be assumed from another broker.

What is the actual spread distribution by hour, at the 17:00-18:00 New York break and reopen, and in the first seconds after payrolls, CPI and FOMC at that broker? No official hourly table was found; the only session-level figures come from unverified vendor pages. This needs to be logged on the live or demo feed.

What are the exact, current event and weekend margin rules at the chosen broker (start and end of the window, leverage during it, whether open positions are recalculated)? Third-party descriptions of these windows contradict each other.

What are CME's gold and silver margin rates today? The latest level found is 5% and 10% after 29 May 2026; changes during the October 2026 sell-off were not checked, and cmegroup.com pages could not be fetched (HTTP 503).
Did standard COMEX GC and SI hours change when CME added 24/7 trading for 1-Ounce Gold and 100-Ounce Silver? No source stated it either way.
Is the IC Markets 1,000-oz silver lot current? The specification sheet is undated; it should be confirmed in the trading terminal's symbol properties.
What are short-side swap rates for gold and silver in late 2026, and how often do brokers change them? Only long-side figures from one September 2026 survey were found.
How much does PCE move metals on its own? It was not measured separately, and the 2026 event samples for payrolls, CPI and FOMC are small (6-7 events each) and come from one broker's hourly bars.

Will the 2026 volatility regime persist? Sixty-day realised volatility (gold 23%, silver 40%) is already below the 250-day figures (28%, 66%), so ATR-based parameters need periodic re-estimation rather than a one-off calibration.

How representative is the OANDA mid-price feed used for the range, gap and session statistics? Weekend-open and post-break prices on another broker can differ, and tick counts are quote updates, not traded volume.

The FCA's final per-asset leverage tiers and the current expiry date of the ASIC product intervention order were not verified from primary text; whether leveraged spot metals are available to retail clients at all in the user's jurisdiction was not checked.

findings.claim: MT5 tick modes differ materially in realism. 'Every tick based on real ticks' replays the broker's recorded Bid/Ask ticks (variable spread inside a minute) and is the only mode MetaQuotes calls 'as close to real conditions as possible'. 'Every tick' synthesises ticks from M1 bars. '1 minute OHLC' and 'Open prices only' fill pending orders, SL and TP at the requested price, which is optimistic. If real ticks are missing, the tester falls back to generated ticks without stopping the run.
findings.evidence: MetaTrader 5 Help (tick generation): generated 'Every tick' uses at most 11 reference points per M1 bar plus interpolated ticks. Real ticks are checked against M1 bars: 'The minute data is considered more reliable', and mismatched ticks for that minute are discarded. 'If a symbol history has a minute bar with no tick data for it, the tester generates ticks' in Every tick mode. Testing-features page: in 'Open prices only' and '1 minute OHLC' modes 'pending orders, as well as SL and TP are executed at the prices specified in the orders'. MQL5 Book: if real ticks are selected and the broker has none, 'All ticks' mode is used, and the tester reports the share of real ticks 'as a percentage (where 100% means all ticks are real)'. Test report: 'History Quality' is the percentage of correct M1 data, with intervals below 50% drawn red. Practical gate (my inference from these documents): final validation only on real ticks, with the real-tick share at or near 100% over the whole window and the first real-tick date checked in the tester journal.

findings.claim: Spread in the MT5 tester is not modelled; it is read from history. With generated ticks there is one fixed spread per M1 bar, and community testing indicates the stored M1 spread is the minute's minimum, so generated-tick and OHLC backtests probably understate real spread cost. This matters most for gold and silver around news and the daily rollover.
findings.evidence: Official documentation: 'During testing, the spread is not modeled but is taken from historical data'; 'In the Strategy Tester, the spread is always considered floating'; for generated ticks 'The Ask price is calculated as Bid + fixed spread of a corresponding minute bar'; if the historical spread is zero or negative the last known spread is used. The 'minimum of the minute' semantics is NOT officially documented. It comes from MQL5 forum tests (a moderator's live M1 monitoring) and a forum statement attributed to a MetaQuotes developer that storage changed from maximum to minimum per minute. Some brokers leave the M1 spread field empty or zero. The documented part is confirmed; the 'minimum' part is community evidence, hence the overall label. The link to gold/silver news and rollover is my inference.

findings.claim: MT5 cost and execution modelling is partial. Commission is configurable in the tester. Execution delay can be zero, fixed (for example measured ping) or random. Swaps appear to use today's symbol specification for the whole history. Delays do not apply to pending, SL or TP triggering. Liquidity, partial fills and real slippage on market orders are not modelled.
findings.evidence: MetaTrader 5 Help (testing): Random Delay draws 0-9 seconds, and 'if a selected number is equal to 9, another number from the same range is selected randomly and added', so 0-8 s with 90% probability and 9-18 s with 10%. Random delay is unavailable in 'Open prices only'. Delays apply only to the EA's trade actions; pending orders are delayed when placed, not when executed. 'No Delay' mode executes 'at requested prices without requotes'. Commission can be per deal or per lot, single or multi-level, charged on entry, exit or both, or copied with 'Use predefined commissions'. 'Almost all specification parameters can be overwritten.' Testing-features page: 'Limit orders are executed at the price specified in the order (without a slippage)', while other types execute at current Bid/Ask ('slippage is possible'). Swaps: no official statement found. An MQL5 forum answer says 'There is no history of swap. Last values will be used for the whole test period', and a September 2026 MQL5 article says the tester 'takes the current swap specification' for the full history. The documented parts are confirmed; the swap behaviour is community-sourced.

findings.claim: MT5's built-in 'Forward' option is a single in-sample/out-of-sample split, not walk-forward analysis. Rolling or anchored walk-forward has to be automated separately. The usual pass marks (walk-forward efficiency of at least 50%, more than half of out-of-sample windows profitable) are conventions, and one peer-reviewed comparison found walk-forward the weakest method at preventing false discoveries.
findings.evidence: MetaTrader 5 Help: forward period options are No, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 or Custom, always the latest part of the range. After optimisation '10% (in the full search) or 25% (in the genetic algorithm) of best runs are selected and tested on the forward period', with a floor of 256 passes. MQL5 article 3279 (Korotky): real walk-forward cannot be launched 'at the touch of a button'; its library supports rolling, anchored and cluster walk-forward, and says 'It is recommended to have a consistency above 50%'. The 50% walk-forward-efficiency rule is attributed to Pardo (2008) only by secondary sources; I could not verify the book's wording. Counter-evidence: Arian, Norouzi Mobarekeh and Seco (Knowledge-Based Systems, 2024; abstract level only) report that Walk-Forward 'exhibits notable shortcomings in false discovery prevention' compared with combinatorial purged cross-validation. My inference: choosing the pass with the best forward result turns the forward segment into in-sample data.

findings.claim: A custom OnTester criterion ('Custom max') lets the optimiser rank passes on a robustness-oriented score, but no criterion removes selection bias. MetaQuotes' own built-in 'Complex Criterion max' has no published formula, and MetaQuotes' book example shows most top in-sample passes failing in the forward period.
findings.evidence: MQL5 docs: OnTester returns a double used as the 'Custom max' criterion, and the genetic algorithm sorts each generation by it. The official sample returns regression slope x trade count / standard error of the balance curve, and 0 if there are fewer than 10 trades. The 10-trade floor is an example, not a recommendation. Optimisation-types page: genetic population 'may range from 64 to 256'; Complex Criterion is 'an integral and complex measure of a test pass quality' weighing number of deals, drawdown, recovery factor, expected payoff and Sharpe ratio. Its formula is not given, and the MQL5 Book notes 'the declared range of 0-100'. In the MQL5 Book's example only about 45% of profitable optimisation passes stayed profitable on the forward period, and 323 of the top 1000. Bailey et al. (PBO paper): 'Any counter-overfitting technique used to select an optimal strategy will result in overfitting.' The MT5 report's Sharpe labels (at least 1.0 'Good', at least 3.0 'Very good') are vendor conventions.

findings.claim: The number of configurations tried must be counted and bounded against data length. With 5 years of data, no more than about 45 independent configurations should be tried before a zero-skill strategy is expected to show an in-sample annualised Sharpe of 1. A typical MT5 optimisation with thousands of passes far exceeds this.
findings.evidence: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu (Notices of the AMS, 2014), Theorem 3.1: MinBTL < 2 ln[N] / E[max_N]^2 (years). 'if only 5 years of data are available, no more than 45 independent model configurations should be tried, or we are almost guaranteed to produce strategies with an annualized Sharpe ratio IS of 1, but an expected Sharpe ratio OOS of zero.' With N = 10, the expected best in-sample Sharpe is 1.57 although the true Sharpe is zero. 'After trying only 7 independent strategy configurations, the expected maximum SR IS is 1 for a 2-year long backtest.' MinBTL is 'a necessary, non-sufficient condition'. 'A researcher that does not report the number of trials N ... makes it impossible to assess the risk of overfitting.' I reproduced these numbers from the formula (N=45 gives 5.00 years; N=10 gives 1.575). My extrapolation with the same formula: 1,000 independent trials need about 10.6 years and 10,000 about 14.9 years. Optimiser passes are correlated, so the effective N is lower than the raw pass count; the paper suggests dimension reduction such as PCA to estimate it.

findings.claim: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is the standard correction for selection among many trials plus non-normal returns. The pass level used in the source paper is DSR of at least 0.95. Even an annualised Sharpe of 2.5 over 5 years of daily data fails once about 100 independent trials are accounted for.
findings.evidence: Bailey and Lopez de Prado (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2014): DSR is a Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio whose benchmark SR0 is the expected maximum Sharpe of N zero-skill trials (extreme-value approximation with the Euler-Mascheroni constant). Inputs are the non-annualised Sharpe, sample length T, skewness, kurtosis, the variance of Sharpe across trials, and the number of independent trials N. In the worked example (annualised SR 2.5, T=1250 daily observations) the investor rejects it 'at a 95% confidence level' because 'there is only a 90% chance that the true SR ... is greater than zero'. With only N=46 trials DSR 'would have been 0.9505'; with Normal returns the same level is reached at N=88. Caveat: my text extraction lost some symbols. The commonly reproduced inputs (N=100, trial-Sharpe variance 1/2, skew -3, kurtosis 10, DSR about 0.90) are from recollection of the paper, not re-read. Appendix A.3 estimates implied independent trials from the average correlation between trials. Related hurdle: Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue a new factor needs 't-ratio greater than 3.0', and Harvey calls the flat 50% Sharpe haircut 'only a rule of thumb' and 'a serious mistake' because the correct haircut is non-linear.

findings.claim: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO), estimated by combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV), measures how often the in-sample best configuration ranks below the median out of sample. The authors' customary rejection level is PBO above 0.05, with S=16 partitions suggested. The same paper explains why a single hold-out is weak evidence.
findings.evidence: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu ('The Probability of Backtest Overfitting'): 'a customary approach would be to reject models for which PBO is estimated to be greater than 0.05'; 'we believe that S = 16 is a reasonable value to use in most cases' (12,780 combinations); the number of trials must be 'N >> 10'. Hold-out critique: it ignores the number of trials; one hold-out has high variance ('Different hold-outs are thus likely to lead to different conclusions'); researchers know what happened in the hold-out period; and hold-out 'should not be applied to an analysis with less than 1,000 observations'. Limitations: all trials must be included ('Hiding trials will lead to an underestimation of the overfit'); it does not validate cost assumptions ('incorrect transaction costs'); and PBO must not be used as the optimisation objective. A March 2026 MQL5 article says PBO cut-offs such as 0.1 or 0.2 'are informal rules of thumb', so only the 0.05 level traces to the paper, and the authors frame even that as customary.

findings.claim: Minimum trade counts (30, 100, 200+) and 'N years of data' rules are conventions without a primary statistical source. The defensible quantities are the Sharpe ratio's standard error and the resulting t-statistic, which show that short backtests and short forward tests carry little statistical information.
findings.evidence: Lo (Financial Analysts Journal, 2002): under IID returns the standard error of the Sharpe estimator is sqrt((1 + SR^2/2)/T), and serial correlation can overstate annualised Sharpe 'by more than 65 percent'. My derivations: the standard error of an annualised Sharpe is roughly 1/sqrt(years), so about +/-1.1 at 95% for a 3-year test. Since t is roughly Sharpe x sqrt(years), t>=2 needs 4 years at Sharpe 1.0 and 1 year at Sharpe 2.0; t>=3 needs 9 years and 2.25 years. A win rate measured on n trades has a 95% half-width of about +/-18 points at n=30, +/-10 at n=100 and +/-5 at n=400. Empirical counter-evidence to trusting backtest metrics: Wiecki et al. (Quantopian, 888 algorithms with at least 6 months out of sample) found backtest Sharpe 'offer[s] little value in predicting out of sample performance (R² < 0.025)' and 'the more backtesting a quant has done for a strategy, the larger the discrepancy'. Conventions found: about 30 trades as a floor and 100+ preferred (forums and blogs); '200+ closed trades is a practical minimum' for Monte Carlo (MQL5 article author); Chan's '252 data points per free parameter' (secondary summary, experience-based, not verified in the book).

findings.claim: Monte Carlo trade resampling (shuffling order, or bootstrap with replacement) is a tool for sizing drawdown risk, not for detecting overfitting. It assumes trades are independent, and every threshold attached to it is a convention.
findings.evidence: Shuffling keeps every trade's profit and loss, so net profit is unchanged and only path metrics such as drawdown vary; an overfitted trade list passes unchanged (logic, plus tool documentation). MQL5 article 22291 (May 2026), bootstrap with replacement, 1,000 runs: 'Bootstrap resampling treats each trade as an independent draw'; 'No serial correlation is modeled between consecutive outcomes'; 'The tool also doesn't model market regime shifts'; 'A 50-trade sample is statistically too thin for stable percentile estimation'. Its example 95th-percentile drawdown was 30.6% against a median of 15.1%, and the author's 1.5-2.5x multiplier over backtest drawdown is personal experience. Bailey et al. note that simulated-scenario approaches carry their own model risk ('the model that generates random series ... may also be overfit'). No peer-reviewed source was found for any Monte Carlo pass/fail threshold; sources are MQL5 articles and vendor documentation.

findings.claim: Choosing a parameter set from a broad plateau rather than an isolated peak is sound practice, but it has no formal threshold. The closest published method is Walton's System Parameter Permutation, which takes the median result across all tested parameter combinations as the realistic expectation.
findings.evidence: MT5 provides 1D, 2D and 3D optimisation graphs with the criterion shown by colour, which is the practical way to see plateaus. Walton, 'Know Your System!' (2014 NAAIM Wagner Award paper; secondary summaries only, primary text not read): the median of each metric across all parameter combinations is treated as the unbiased estimate, with best and worst as the optimistic and pessimistic bounds. Critics note that the parameter ranges must be fixed in advance and that changing them after seeing results re-introduces snooping. The rationale agrees with Bailey et al.: the maximum of many trials is biased upward, while a central value of the distribution is not. Rules such as 'neighbours within +/-10-20% must stay profitable' are practitioner convention; I found no primary source for a number.

findings.claim: Gold and silver backtests are broker-specific. Spot metals are over-the-counter with no single price, the MT5 tester only uses the connected broker's own M1 and tick history, and real-tick depth varies by broker. A result on one broker's data is one sample, and cross-feed testing needs custom symbols or accounts at other brokers.
findings.evidence: LBMA OTC Guide: members trade 'on a principal-to-principal, or bilateral, basis', 'known as an OTC market as opposed to an exchange traded environment'. MetaTrader 5 Help: 'From the trading server, M1 bars and tick data for the selected symbol are downloaded to the terminal'; if history is short 'the tester automatically shifts the actual start date forward'. Custom symbols accept bar and tick imports from text files and can be tested on local agents, but not on the MQL5 Cloud Network, and 'Real trades cannot be executed on custom symbols'. Broker differences in gold spread: an industry comparison reported one broker's average gold spread about 2.56 times another's (a broker-affiliated study, indicative only). Real-tick history depth being 'a few years' at many brokers is a community claim; I found no official figure. MT5's 'All symbols selected in Market Watch' mode runs the same inputs on other symbols, which gives a cheap XAGUSD-versus-XAUUSD robustness check.

findings.claim: Known tester pitfalls: the MQL5 economic calendar is only available online, not in the tester; TimeGMT() in the tester equals server time, so GMT-offset and session logic silently break; broker server time usually switches between GMT+2 and GMT+3 on the US daylight-saving schedule; bars of different symbols are not synchronised; and WebRequest and alerts do not run in the tester.
findings.evidence: MQL5 Book: 'The calendar is available for MQL programs only online'; the workaround is a cache file saved on a live chart and loaded with #property tester_file. Archived event times follow the server's current zone, so events from the opposite daylight-saving half-year need a one-hour correction. MQL5 docs: calendar functions 'use the trade server time'; 'During testing in the strategy tester, TimeGMT() is always equal to TimeTradeServer() simulated server time'; TimeLocal() also equals server time in the tester. Broker documentation (Darwinex): 'Time in Metatrader terminals is set to New York Close', GMT+3 during US summertime and GMT+2 otherwise. This is common but broker-specific, and US and European clock changes are out of step for a few weeks each spring and autumn. Multi-symbol: 'a new bar for each symbol is opened, regardless of how the bar opened on another symbol'; the Book recommends waiting until all symbols' last bars have equal open times. Not executed in the tester: Alert, MessageBox, PlaySound, SendMail, SendNotification, SendFTP, WebRequest. Recent 2026 release notes surfaced in search (builds 5640 to 6230) mention no calendar support in the tester, but I did not check every build.

findings.claim: No authoritative source sets a demo or forward-test duration. The principled measure is the Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL), which implies that a 1-3 month demo cannot statistically confirm an edge unless the Sharpe ratio is very high. Demo runs mainly test implementation and execution parity; practitioner 'incubation' of 3-12 months is convention.
findings.evidence: Bailey and Lopez de Prado (Journal of Risk, 2012), formula via a secondary reproduction: MinTRL = 1 + [1 - skew x SR + (kurtosis - 1)/4 x SR^2] x (z / (SR - SR*))^2, in observations, with SR per observation. My calculations for daily returns at 95% confidence against SR* = 0, Normal returns: annualised Sharpe 1.0 needs about 684 trading days (2.7 years); 1.5 needs about 305 days (1.2 years); 2.0 needs about 173 days (0.7 years); 3.0 needs about 78 days (0.3 years). Negative skew and fat tails lengthen these. Conventions: Kevin Davey's incubation is reported as 3 months to 6-12 months depending on the source (podcast and forum summaries, not his book). Regulatory context: CFTC Rule 4.41(b) requires simulated results to carry a statement that they 'have certain inherent limitations'. ESMA reports '74-89% of retail accounts typically lose money' on CFDs, with 'average losses per client ranging from €1,600 to €29,000'. That demo accounts understate slippage and requotes is supported only by educational and forum sources; I found no official broker disclosure.

implications_for_bot: Data gate (sourced mechanics, my thresholds): run final validation only in 'Every tick based on real ticks' on the broker and account type that will be traded live. Require the real-tick share at or near 100% and History Quality well above the 50% red level for the whole window, and find the first real-tick date for XAUUSD and XAGUSD in the tester journal. Treat anything before that date as generated-tick data with understated spread.

Cost gate: set commission explicitly, or use 'Use predefined commissions' and check it against the live contract specification. Run with a fixed delay equal to measured ping and again with Random Delay. Add a stress run with spread widened and swaps raised, because the tester appears to apply today's swap to all history and does not model slippage or liquidity. If the edge disappears under a modest cost stress, fail it. The stress multipliers are convention, not sourced.

Trial budget: log every optimisation pass and every manual variant as a trial. With about 5 years of metals data, the published bound is roughly 45 independent configurations for a zero-skill in-sample Sharpe of 1. Keep optimised parameters few and grids coarse, prefer the slow complete search on a small grid over large genetic runs, and export all passes so the trial count and Sharpe dispersion are available for DSR.

Statistical gates with a primary source: DSR of at least 0.95 using an honest trial count, and PBO by CSCV (S=16) of at most 0.05 as the strict level. These need per-pass return series exported from MT5 and computed outside the tester, since MT5 has no built-in DSR or PBO. A t-statistic of at least 3 (annualised Sharpe times the square root of years) is the stricter hurdle when many variants were tried. Treat the informal PBO levels of 0.1-0.2 as a softer band, not a pass.

Convention-only gates, to be labelled as such in the bot's validation report: walk-forward efficiency of at least 50%, more than 50% of out-of-sample windows profitable, at least 100-200 trades in sample and at least 30 per out-of-sample window, neighbouring parameter values still profitable, and Monte Carlo 95th-percentile drawdown inside the risk budget. Size positions from the Monte Carlo drawdown, not the single backtest drawdown.

Walk-forward: MT5's Forward option is one split and re-tests only the top 10% or 25% of passes. Use it as a quick screen, then run a scripted rolling or anchored walk-forward. Keep one final holdout that is opened once, and do not pick parameters by forward-tab rank, because that makes the forward data in-sample.

OnTester: use a custom criterion that returns 0 below a minimum trade count and rewards a smooth equity curve and low drawdown, in the style of the official example. Do not rely on 'Complex Criterion max', whose formula is unpublished. Read the 2D/3D optimisation surface and take the centre of a plateau, or use the median across the parameter set as the expected result.

Gold and silver specifics: prices are OTC and broker-specific, so re-test on at least one other feed (a second broker account or imported ticks as a custom symbol) and run the same inputs on XAGUSD as a robustness check. A strategy that works only on one broker's XAUUSD history should be treated as fitted to that feed.

Time and news handling: do not use TimeGMT() or TimeGMTOffset logic in backtests, because in the tester TimeGMT() equals server time. Derive session times from server time with an explicit broker offset table that follows the US daylight-saving schedule, and verify it around the March and October-November changeovers. A news filter needs a calendar cache file with daylight-saving correction; otherwise the filter is silently inactive in the tester and the backtest does not represent the live bot.
Multi-symbol logic (for example a gold/silver ratio): check that the last bars of all symbols have equal open times before acting, and do not test such logic in 'Open prices only' mode.

Demo and go-live: treat demo as an implementation and execution-parity test. Re-run the tester over the demo period and compare trade by trade (entries, fills, spread, slippage). Statistical confirmation needs the MinTRL length, roughly 0.7 years at Sharpe 2 and 2.7 years at Sharpe 1, so plan a staged start with minimum size on live and pre-written stop rules, such as live drawdown beyond the Monte Carlo 95th percentile. The 3-6 month incubation figure is convention.

Set expectations from the evidence: backtest Sharpe had almost no power to predict live results in the Quantopian cohort (R² below 0.025), and 74-89% of retail CFD accounts lose money. A passed validation pipeline lowers the chance of a false positive; it does not show the bot is profitable.
open_questions: How far back does the target broker's real-tick history go for XAUUSD and XAGUSD, and how does its recorded spread compare with live spread at rollover and around major news? This can only be answered by a tick audit on the actual account.

What exactly does the MT5 M1 bar 'spread' field store (minimum, open or last of the minute) on current builds and at the target broker? MetaQuotes has not documented it; the 'minimum' reading is community evidence.

Does the tester apply only the current swap specification to all history on current builds, and how does it handle the triple-swap day and percentage-mode swaps for metals? No official statement was found.

Has any 2026 MT5 build added economic-calendar support in the Strategy Tester? The MQL5 Book says the calendar is online-only and the release notes I saw do not mention a change, but I did not review every build.

How should the effective number of independent trials be estimated for MT5 genetic optimisations, where passes are highly correlated? The DSR paper offers an average-correlation method, but it needs per-pass return series, which the standard XML export does not include.
How does MT5 compute its reported Sharpe ratio (sampling period and annualisation)? It may not be directly usable as the per-observation Sharpe that DSR and MinTRL require.
Pardo's 50% walk-forward-efficiency threshold and Chan's '252 observations per free parameter' rule were found only in secondary sources; the original book wording was not verified.

The DSR worked-example inputs (N=100, trial-Sharpe variance 1/2, skew -3, kurtosis 10) were not legible in my text extraction of the paper and are quoted from recollection; T=1250, the 0.9505 result at N=46 and the '90% chance' statement were read directly.
What is the live slippage and requote distribution for market and stop orders in gold at the target broker? Neither the tester nor a demo account measures it; only small-size live trading will.

Is PBO at or below 0.05 achievable for a small retail parameter grid, given that the method needs many trials (N much greater than 10) and at least a few years of data for S=16 partitions? It may be too strict or too noisy at this scale.

findings.claim: Binance USD-M futures does list XAUUSDT (gold) and XAGUSDT (silver) perpetuals, and both were still trading on 2026-11-13. XAUUSDT first traded on 2025-12-11 (thin soft launch) and was opened to all eligible markets on 2026-01-05; XAGUSDT started 2026-01-07 10:00 UTC. They are USDT-margined, no-expiry 'TradFi Perpetual Contracts' offered through Nest Exchange Limited, a Binance entity regulated by ADGM's FSRA.
findings.evidence: Binance's public data archive holds XAUUSDT aggTrades/klines/funding files from 2025-12 to daily files dated 2026-11-13, and XAGUSDT from 2026-01. First XAUUSDT 1-minute bar is 2025-12-11 08:05 UTC; December 2025 volume was only about $0.08B and 31% of minute bars had no trades. First XAGUSDT bar is 2026-01-07 10:00 UTC. Trade prints show a 0.01 USDT price increment and 0.001 oz quantity increment. Binance's 2026-01-08 press release names Nest Exchange Limited (FSRA Recognised Investment Exchange) and says fees follow the existing perpetual structure; the 5 Jan / 7 Jan general-availability dates come from secondary coverage. The Binance API changelog of 2025-12-11 added GET /fapi/v1/tradingSchedule and POST /fapi/v1/stock/contract (sign TradFi-Perps agreement). Not verified: max leverage (reports say 50x at silver launch) and min notional (reported 5 USDT), because the exchangeInfo endpoint returned HTTP 451 from my location.

findings.claim: Liquidity on Binance's gold perp is now large and the quoted spread is one tick. Silver is thinner and its 0.01 tick is coarse relative to price (about 2 bps).
findings.evidence: Computed by me from Binance archive files. XAUUSDT: about $51.8B quote volume in October 2026 (about $2.26B per weekday, $244M per weekend day), zero no-trade minutes; on Thu 2026-11-12 volume was $2.75B, open interest $441-541M, resting depth within +/-0.2% about $8M per side, and the spread inferred from alternating-aggressor trades was 0.01 USDT (about 0.025 bps). XAGUSDT: about $20.5B in October 2026 (about $876M per weekday, $133M per weekend day); on 2026-11-12 open interest was about $220-240M, depth within +/-0.2% about $3.3M per side, spread one tick of 0.01 on a roughly $51 price (about 1.9 bps). Binance's PAXGUSDT perp did about $2.07B in October 2026, roughly 4% of XAUUSDT. The spread figure is an estimate from trade data, not a book snapshot.

findings.claim: The Binance metals perps trade 24/7, including Saturdays and Sundays, but weekend liquidity is a small fraction of weekday liquidity and the index/mark mechanics differ when the underlying market is closed. Those off-hours mechanics were changed twice in 2026, so the short price history spans different regimes.
findings.evidence: Confirmed from archive data: XAUUSDT traded in every hour of Sat 2026-11-07 ($159M) and Sun 2026-11-08 ($449M) versus $2,746M on Thu 2026-11-12. One blog describes a '24/5 model' from 2026-09-15; the trade data contradicts that reading, so it most plausibly refers to the underlying/index session (reported as Sun 18:00 ET to Fri 17:00 ET with the daily break removed). At launch the price index was frozen at its last value off-hours and the mark price used an EWMA with a deviation cap (for example +/-3% for XAUUSDT). From 2026-05-08 21:00 UTC commodity contracts moved to an 'Orderbook EWMA' index off-hours, which Binance said makes off-hours liquidation behaviour track exchange liquidity (secondary coverage of a Binance notice). Observed weekend behaviour, Fri 21:00 to Sun 22:00 UTC: in Sep-Oct 2026 XAUUSDT moved at most 0.42% with weekend high-low ranges up to 0.75%; XAGUSDT weekend ranges reached 2.4% in October 2026 and 4.6% in January 2026.

findings.claim: Funding on the Binance metals perps settles every 4 hours, has mostly been paid by longs, was very expensive in the first months and is modest now. It is zero about half the time and can spike on weekends.
findings.evidence: Computed from Binance's fundingRate archive. XAUUSDT: 4-hour interval in every month through October 2026 (one isolated 8-hour record on 2026-01-30). Cumulative funding from 2025-12-11 to 2026-10-31 was +11.2% paid by longs, of which January 2026 alone was +4.35%. April-October 2026 summed to +1.97% (about 3.4% annualised); July-October 2026 summed to +2.13% (about 6.3% annualised). XAGUSDT: +16.2% cumulative from 2026-01-07, +4.3% for April-October 2026 (about 7.4% annualised). Extremes: +0.5% per 4 hours (hit on Saturday 2026-02-28) and -0.34% (gold) / -0.40% (silver). In October 2026, 94 of 186 gold prints were exactly zero and none were negative. A January 2026 news report that funding moved to 8-hourly with a +/-0.05% cap is not consistent with this data. Perp premium over index in October 2026 averaged +0.04% for gold (range -0.26% to +0.18%) and +0.04% for silver (range -0.80% to +0.42%).

findings.claim: Cost structures are opposite: on Binance the exchange fee dominates and the spread is negligible, while on a raw-spread CFD account the spread plus a small commission dominates. For market-order (taker) trading in gold, Binance is roughly an order of magnitude more expensive per round trip than a raw CFD account.
findings.evidence: Binance says TradFi perps use the same fee structure as its other perpetuals; a Binance support example uses 0.02% maker and 0.05% taker for a regular user, with a 10% discount when paying fees in BNB. At about $3,900 gold, 0.05% is about $1.95 per ounce per side, so about $3.90 per ounce (10 bps) round trip as taker and about $1.56 as maker. Pepperstone's own gold page quotes Razor raw spreads 'as low as 0.08' plus $3.50 per lot per side; on a standard 100-oz lot that commission is $0.07 per ounce round trip. Even if the average spread is several times the minimum, the CFD round trip is likely well under $0.50 per ounce (about 1 bp). Caveats: I did not find an official average-spread or swap-rate figure, the 100-oz lot size is the usual MT5 convention rather than something stated on that page, and I could not load Binance's live fee table, so the account's actual rate should be read from the API. Holding cost is funding (floating, every 4 hours, can be zero or received) on perps versus a daily broker-set swap on CFDs; CFD swap levels were not verified.

findings.claim: Access to the Binance metals perps is restricted by jurisdiction and requires a one-time TradFi-Perps agreement; the futures API is also geo-blocked at the network level, so the server's location matters. ccxt already exposes the relevant Binance endpoints.
findings.evidence: A request to fapi.binance.com/fapi/v1/exchangeInfo from my US-located environment returned HTTP 451 'Service unavailable from a restricted location according to b. Eligibility'. Binance's API changelog lists POST /fapi/v1/stock/contract (and a portfolio-margin equivalent added 2026-04-08) to 'sign TradFi-Perps agreement contract'. The current ccxt master source (ccxt 4.5.92, released 2026-11-04) includes 'stock/contract' and 'tradingSchedule' in its Binance endpoint map and classifies a market as a swap when contractType is PERPETUAL or the expiry is the perpetual sentinel. Not verified: the exact list of excluded countries (secondary sources mention the US), the unified ccxt symbol for these contracts, and the error returned when the agreement is unsigned.

findings.claim: Other large venues have equivalent gold and silver perps, but with far less volume than Binance. OKX and Hyperliquid are live and reachable by API; Bybit lists them but geo-blocks more aggressively.
findings.evidence: OKX public API on 2026-11-14 about 12:56 UTC (a Saturday): XAU-USDT-SWAP live, tick 0.1, contract value 0.001 XAU, max leverage 100, funding cap +/-0.75% with 8-hour settlement, open interest about $173M, 24-hour volume about 51,226 oz (about $199M); XAG-USDT-SWAP listed 2026-01-28, 24-hour volume about 1.13M oz (about $55M). OKX's help page says the index blends traditional sources with Binance, Hyperliquid and OKX perp prices and leans on the crypto perps off-hours, capped at +/-10% of the last traditional close. Hyperliquid API (builder market 'xyz'): xyz:GOLD max leverage 25, open interest about $290M, day volume about $35M; xyz:SILVER open interest about $153M, day volume about $84M; funding 0.000625% per hour at that moment. Bybit's v5 docs list XAUUSDT and XAGUSDT commodity perps that require an agreement signed by the master account, and state its MT5 gold CFD (XAUUSD.s) is not available through the v5 API; Bybit's API refused my location outright and its March 2026 launch date is from secondary coverage only. ccxt's Hyperliquid module has explicit HIP-3 market support.

findings.claim: Tokenised gold (PAXG) is a usable but imperfect proxy: it tracks gold with a floating basis of a few tenths of a percent and far lower liquidity than the XAUUSDT perp. There is no comparably established tokenised silver.
findings.evidence: Computed from Binance archive 1-minute closes for October 2026: the PAXGUSDT perp versus the XAUUSDT perp averaged -0.06% with a range of -0.38% to +0.23% (standard deviation 0.14%, wider on weekends). A single weekend snapshot on OKX showed spot PAXG-USDT at 3,866.3 against its gold perp at 3,882.5 (about -0.4%). Binance has listed a PAXGUSDT perp since March 2025. Paxos is a New York trust company supervised by NYDFS and each token represents one fine troy ounce held in London; Paxos' fee pages show a new tiered creation/redemption schedule from 2026-09-01. The roughly 430-token minimum for physical bar redemption comes from secondary sources. I did not search specifically for tokenised silver products, so the silver statement is an absence of evidence, not a verified negative.

findings.claim: The official MetaTrader5 Python package is Windows-only and is a request/response bridge to a locally running terminal. It cannot use the MT5 Strategy Tester, has no event callbacks, and cannot run on MetaQuotes' built-in VPS, so it does not fit a Linux PaaS.
findings.evidence: PyPI shows MetaTrader5 5.0.6231 (released 2026-09-27) with nine wheels, all tagged Windows x86-64 (CPython 3.6 to 3.14) and no source distribution. The official docs list 32 functions: connect/login, account and symbol info, market depth, copy_rates_* bars, copy_ticks_* ticks, order_check/order_send, positions and history. There are no tester or event-handler functions, and initialize() takes a path to the terminal .exe and launches it. MetaQuotes officially supports the MT5 terminal on Linux only through Wine (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint, Fedora). The built-in MQL5 VPS forbids DLL calls and does not migrate scripts, so a Python process cannot live there; a full Windows VPS is needed. That the Strategy Tester only runs MQL5 programs is stated by MQL5 forum moderators rather than in the docs page I read, so that part is very likely rather than documented. Community Wine or remote-bridge packages exist but are unofficial.

findings.claim: The MT5 Strategy Tester is the strongest ready-made backtesting tool among the options, but only for strategies written in MQL5, and its 'real ticks' are that broker's own tick history with documented gaps-filling behaviour.
findings.evidence: Official MT5 help: modelling modes are Every tick, Every tick based on real ticks, 1 minute OHLC, Open prices only and Math calculations; a forward option splits the period 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 or at a custom date and re-tests the best passes out of sample; execution delay can be none, random, or fixed to measured ping; multi-symbol testing is automatic; one local agent runs per logical CPU core, remote agents can be added, and optimisation offers a complete search or a genetic algorithm with 1D/2D/3D result views. Real ticks are those 'accumulated by a broker'; when a minute has no ticks the tester generates them, and minute data is treated as more reliable when they disagree. MQL5 Cloud Network costs $0.08 per hour for an agent of productivity 100 plus $0.00002 per MB of traffic, with a 4 GB RAM/disk limit per pass. Forum users report cloud bills from cents to over $150 for large runs. How many years of real ticks exist for gold or silver depends on the broker and was not verified.

findings.claim: Free tick-level history exists for every route, but its depth and nature differ: Binance publishes full trade history for its metals perps (only since December 2025), while long histories come from spot/CFD or futures sources that are different instruments.
findings.evidence: Binance's archive offers free aggTrades, trades, klines, funding rates, mark/index/premium klines, book depth and open-interest metrics for XAUUSDT and XAGUSDT, about 11 months for gold and 10 for silver. Dukascopy says its export tool provides free data from tick-by-tick upward for forex, commodities and indices; the page does not name gold/silver or state the start year, though third-party tools list XAU/USD and XAG/USD. OANDA's v20 API provides historical pricing back to 2005 as candles rather than raw ticks. Databento sells CME Globex data including gold futures on usage-based historical pricing with $125 of free credit. MT5 supplies the connected broker's ticks. Inference: a Python backtest of the Binance contract over more than one year must use a proxy series and add fees, funding and weekend behaviour by assumption.

findings.claim: OANDA v20 and cTrader are the broker routes that run natively from Linux with Python. OANDA is a plain REST and streaming API but is not available in every OANDA division; cTrader offers both an external Open API and a command-line tool that runs and backtests bots on Linux.
findings.evidence: OANDA developer docs: token-authenticated REST plus streaming hosts, 120 requests per second and 20 streams per IP, at most 2 new connections per second, a practice environment, and v20 accounts 'available to all divisions except OANDA Global Markets and OANDA TMS BROKERS S.A.'. Metals availability per division was not verified. cTrader: the Open API uses JSON or Protobuf over TCP/WebSocket with limits of 50 requests per second (5 for historical data), any language, with an official Python SDK built on Twisted. The cTrader CLI docs say it can 'run, stop and backtest cBots' on Windows, macOS and Linux without the desktop app, with a Docker image; native Python bots arrived in cTrader 5.4 (August 2025). Not verified: whether Python bots backtest on tick data under the Linux CLI, and forum users report slow tick-data loading.

findings.claim: Interactive Brokers gives access to exchange-traded micro futures and spot metals, but its API depends on a GUI gateway process that must stay running, and micro futures are coarse for a small account.
findings.evidence: IBKR's API docs state there must be a running TWS or IB Gateway instance, that headless operation is not supported, that it restarts daily (auto-restart since version 974) and that credentials must be re-entered after the Saturday-night server reset. IBKR's metals page (seen via search snippets; the page itself returned 403) lists spot gold at 1.5 bps of trade value with a $2 minimum up to $500k and 0.10% per year storage. CME: Micro Gold (MGC) is 10 troy ounces with a $0.10 tick worth $1; Micro Silver (SIL) is 1,000 troy ounces with a $0.005 outright tick worth $5 per the COMEX rulebook, trading Sunday to Friday 6 pm to 5 pm ET with a one-hour daily break. CME pages returned 503 to me, so these come from search results of CME documents and one CME page reportedly shows a different silver tick. At about $3,900 gold one MGC is about $39,000 notional, versus a 0.001-oz (about $4) increment on Binance. IBKR micro commissions of $0.10-0.25 per contract plus exchange fees come from a 2025 IBKR page and were not re-verified.

findings.claim: Counterparty and regulatory protection varies widely across the routes: exchange-cleared futures and EU/UK-regulated CFDs carry the most retail protection, offshore CFD entities and crypto venues carry less, and Hyperliquid's builder markets depend on a single deployer's oracle.
findings.evidence: ESMA's 2018 measures capped retail CFD leverage at 20:1 for gold and 10:1 for other commodities such as silver, with a 50% margin close-out rule and negative balance protection; the FCA made equivalent rules permanent in PS19/18. I did not re-check their current status. Pepperstone's UAE-facing gold page names Pepperstone Markets Limited (Securities Commission of The Bahamas) as product issuer, illustrating that the contracting entity may be offshore. Binance's metals perps are issued by an ADGM-regulated exchange entity but settle in USDT, so profit and loss carry stablecoin exposure, and access is jurisdiction-gated. Hyperliquid's HIP-3 docs say the deployer defines and sets the oracle price, leverage limits and can halt trading, backed by a slashable 500k HYPE stake. A CFD broker is the direct counterparty to each trade; that last point is general market structure rather than something I sourced here.

implications_for_bot: The existing Python + ccxt Binance-futures bot on Linux makes Binance XAUUSDT/XAGUSDT the lowest-friction route by a wide margin: same API, same margin wallet, same deployment. The new work is a one-time TradFi-Perps agreement (web UI or POST /fapi/v1/stock/contract), confirming the account's jurisdiction is eligible, and checking how the installed ccxt version names the markets after load_markets().

Every MetaTrader route breaks that setup. An MQL5 Expert Advisor means rewriting the strategy in a new language, and the official Python package needs a Windows host with a running terminal, so neither runs on a Linux PaaS or on MetaQuotes' built-in VPS. Budget a Windows VPS if that route is chosen.

Model costs as fee-dominated on Binance: about 10 bps (roughly $3.90 per ounce of gold) per taker round trip against a one-tick spread. Strategies with small targets per trade that work on a raw-spread CFD account will likely not survive taker fees; prefer post-only/limit entries, fewer trades and larger targets, and read the real commission rate for the symbol from the API before sizing.

Add funding to the P&L model as a 4-hourly cash flow using Binance's published funding history. Recent levels are modest (roughly 3-7% a year paid by longs) but early 2026 was far higher and single prints reached +0.5% per 4 hours on a weekend, so cap position size or flatten ahead of funding when the premium is stretched.

Treat weekends and off-hours as a separate regime. The contract trades 24/7 but with roughly 6-16% of weekday volume and an order-book-based index, so add session awareness (GET /fapi/v1/tradingSchedule), smaller size or no new entries off-hours, and an explicit rule for the Sunday reopen. Silver needs stricter rules than gold because its weekend ranges and tick size are much larger in relative terms.

Backtest in Python on Binance's own archive (aggTrades, 1-minute klines, funding, premium index, book depth) for execution realism, but note it only covers 10-11 months and includes two changes to off-hours pricing (2026-05-08 and 2026-09-15) and an illiquid first month. For longer history use spot gold/silver ticks or CME futures as a proxy and validate the proxy against the 2026 overlap.

To approximate what MT5's tester gives for free, the Python backtester needs an event-driven fill model with fees, funding, tick size and minimum order size, a walk-forward split equivalent to MT5's forward mode, and parallel parameter search across CPU cores. A framework with a Binance adapter and shared backtest/live code (for example NautilusTrader, which lists Binance, Bybit, OKX, Hyperliquid and Interactive Brokers as stable integrations) is an alternative to building this.

MT5 can still be used as a research tool only: prototype logic in the Strategy Tester on a broker's long gold/silver tick history, then port to Python for Binance. Results will not transfer one-to-one because the CFD has a spread-plus-swap cost model and weekend closure, while the perp has fees, funding and weekend trading.
