Other brokers: IG lists 100 troy oz for gold ($100 per point) and 5,000 troy oz for silver ($5,000 per point). Fusion Markets lists '100 oz of Gold' and '5000 oz of Silver'. Finance Magnates confirms VT Markets' XAUUSD247 is a one-ounce contract against 100 oz for standard XAUUSD.

The report's arithmetic is right: one gold lot is about $388k, one 5,000-oz silver lot about $244k, and at current ATR(14) a 0.01 lot swings about $90 per day in gold and about $108 in silver.

Caveats:
- The 1,000-oz figure is what one undated IC document says. The same sheet carries a spread table that disagrees with IC's live site, and IC's live commodities page states no contract size, so the live XAGUSD lot size is unconfirmed. It must be read from the symbol properties in the terminal.
- 'Every broker checked' is four brokers.

This supports the design rule to read contract size, tick value and volume step from the broker at run time and never hard-code them.

checked.claim: Margin: regulated retail CFD accounts are capped at 20:1 on gold (5% margin) and 10:1 on silver (10%, as a 'commodity other than gold') with a 50% margin close-out; offshore entities advertise up to 1:1000-1:2000. Exchange margins show how fast requirements move: CME switched to percentage-of-notional margins in January 2026 and moved gold between 5% and 9% and silver between 10% and 18% within five months. Brokers follow, sometimes with days of notice and applied to open positions.
checked.note:
Confirmed from the pages themselves:
- ESMA: '20:1 for non-major currency pairs, gold and major indices', '10:1 for commodities other than gold and non-major equity indices', close-out 'at 50% of minimum required margin'.
- ASIC: the same 20:1 and 10:1 limits, 'From 29 March 2021'.
- CME via Kitco: percentage-of-contract-value margins from 13 Jan 2026 (gold 5%, silver 9%); raised 'to 9% from 8%' for gold and 'to 18% from 15%' for silver after the close on 6 Feb 2026. Via Angel One: cut from 6% to 5% and from 11% to 10% after the close on 29 May 2026.
- OANDA Japan (Finance Magnates): silver margin 5% to 20% from 2 Feb 2026 for existing and new positions, maximum order 10 lots to 5 lots, position cap cut 75%, warning of forced liquidation at the Monday open and possible suspension of silver trading.
- IC sheet: max leverage 1:2000 for gold, 1:1000 for silver.

Two corrections, neither changes the design conclusion:
- Silver's CME range was 9% to 18%, not 10% to 18%: it started at 9% on 13 January.
- 'Regulated retail accounts' means the EU, UK and Australia. Other regulated venues differ: OANDA Japan had silver at 20:1 until February 2026, and IG's international page shows 0.5% margin on gold and 2% on silver.

Not verified:
- The FCA press release states only 'between 30:1 and 2:1' and the 50% close-out; it gives no per-asset tiers.
- The CME figures come from press coverage, not CME advisories (cmegroup.com returned 503), and the latest level found is still 29 May 2026. Current CME margins after the October sell-off are unknown.
- Whether the ASIC order is still in force in its 2021 form.

Spread: no book snapshot is available to me (the live API is geo-blocked), so I re-ran the trade-based inference independently. For consecutive opposite-aggressor trades within one second, the price gap was exactly 0.01 in 77% of gold pairs and 62% of silver pairs (a further 38% of silver pairs were 0.00), which is consistent with a one-tick spread but remains an estimate. 0.01 on a silver price of about $50-52 is about 1.9-2.0 bps. checked.note: I recomputed everything from Binance's fundingRate archive and the figures match. XAUUSDT: 1,947 records, all 4-hour except one 8-hour record on 2026-01-30; cumulative +11.24% from 2025-12-11 to 2026-10-31; January 2026 alone +4.35%; April-October +1.97% (3.4% annualised); July-October +2.13% (6.4% annualised); maximum +0.50% on Saturday 2026-02-28 12:00 UTC; minimum -0.335%. checked.claim: Cost structures are opposite: on Binance the exchange fee dominates and the spread is negligible, while on a raw-spread CFD account the spread plus a small commission dominates. For market-order (taker) trading in gold, Binance is roughly an order of magnitude more expensive per round trip than a raw CFD account (about $3.90 per ounce, 10 bps, versus well under $0.50).
checked.note: The inputs check out against primary pages, with one citation error. The Binance FAQ URL cited in the report does not contain the fee rates; the sibling page 'Binance Futures Fee Structure & Fee Calculations' does state a Regular User maker fee of 0.02% and taker fee of 0.05%, and a 10% discount when paying in BNB. The press release says TradFi perps follow the existing perpetual fee structure. Pepperstone's page confirms raw gold spreads 'from 0.08' and $3.50 per lot per side. I also found the average spread the report was missing: Pepperstone's commodity-fees page lists Spot Gold on Razor at 0.08 minimum and 0.12 average (Standard: 0.19 and 0.23). With a 100-oz lot, the CFD round trip is about $0.12 + $0.07 = $0.19 per ounce (about 0.5 bps at $3,900), against $3.90 as a Binance taker, so the gap is about 20 times for takers and about 8 times maker-to-maker. The claim holds and is, if anything, understated. Still unverified: the 100-oz lot size (not stated on the Pepperstone pages I read; it is the usual MT5 convention), CFD swap rates, spreads at other Pepperstone entities or in fast markets, and the fee rate this specific Binance account actually pays on these symbols.

checked.claim: The official MetaTrader5 Python package is Windows-only and is a request/response bridge to a locally running terminal. It cannot use the MT5 Strategy Tester, has no event callbacks, and cannot run on MetaQuotes' built-in VPS, so it does not fit a Linux PaaS.
checked.note: PyPI's own metadata confirms version 5.0.6231, uploaded 2026-09-27, with exactly nine files, all win_amd64 wheels for CPython 3.6 to 3.14 and no source distribution, so pip cannot install it on Linux. The official MQL5 documentation page lists 32 functions (connection, account and symbol info, market depth, copy_rates and copy_ticks, order_check and order_send, positions and history) and describes the package as interprocess communication 'directly from the MetaTrader 5 terminal'; there are no Strategy Tester or event-handler functions. MetaQuotes' Linux page says the terminal 'runs on Linux using Wine' (Ubuntu, Debian, Linux Mint, Fedora). The virtual hosting page states 'DLL calls are completely forbidden in the virtual platform' and 'Scripts cannot be moved during migration'. Two parts rest on inference, not an explicit statement: 'cannot use the Strategy Tester' follows from the absence of any tester function in the docs, and 'cannot run on the built-in VPS' follows from the DLL ban and the VPS only hosting the terminal's own programs (that page does not mention Python). I found nothing that contradicts either. Unofficial Wine-based workarounds exist but were not evaluated.

checked.claim: Order filling policy must be chosen at runtime from SYMBOL_FILLING_MODE plus SYMBOL_TRADE_EXEMODE; hard-coding FOK, IOC or RETURN will be rejected on some brokers (retcode 10030 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_FILL).
checked.note: Re-read the MQL5 reference pages directly. Confirmed: SYMBOL_FILLING_FOK=1, IOC=2, BOC=4; the per-execution-mode table reads exactly as reported (Instant/Request: FOK and IOC 'regardless of a symbol setting', RETURN 'always'; Market: FOK/IOC 'set in the symbol settings', RETURN 'disabled regardless of the symbol settings'; Exchange: FOK/IOC per symbol, RETURN always). The docs also state 'Return orders are not allowed in the Market Execution mode' and that pending orders should use ORDER_FILLING_RETURN 'regardless of an execution type'. Retcode 10030 = 'Invalid order filling type' and 10010 = 'Only part of the request was completed' confirmed. The MQL5 Book confirms the execution mode 'is predetermined by the broker for each symbol'. Could not refute. Caveats: (1) no public per-broker table of filling flags exists, so which case applies on the user's gold/silver symbol is still unknown until read live; (2) the docs do not cover the edge case where the symbol's filling flags read as 0, so the selector should have a defined fallback. Method note: the web-search budget for this run was exhausted, so this check used direct fetches of primary documentation rather than independent searches.

checked.claim: OrderSend() returning true is not execution; the EA must branch on MqlTradeResult.retcode. Requotes belong to Instant Execution; in Market Execution the price and deviation fields are not required, so the 'slippage' parameter is not a protection there.
checked.note: Confirmed on primary pages. OrderSend docs: true means 'a successful basic check of structures' and 'this is not a sign of successful execution of a trade operation'; 'we should first check the retcode'. MqlTradeRequest docs: Instant/Request require action, symbol, volume, price, sl, tp, deviation, type, type_filling; Market/Exchange require only action, symbol, volume, type, type_filling. MT5 help: Instant Execution sends a 'Requote' if the price is rejected; in Market Execution the broker decides the price 'without any additional discussion with a trader' and sending the order 'means advance consent'. The 'slippage is not a protection' part was labelled an inference in the report, but I found it stated outright in the official MQL5 Book: 'The deviation field affects the execution of market orders only in the Instant Execution and Request Execution modes.' So that point is stronger than the report claimed. All listed retcodes (10004, 10006, 10012, 10020, 10021, 10024, 10028, 10031, 10017, 10018, 10026, 10027) match the official table. Not verified and not verifiable: the transient / re-compute / terminal retry classification is the report's own design choice; MetaQuotes publishes no retry policy. Search budget was exhausted, so no independent search for broker-specific exceptions was possible.

checked.claim: The same metal is a different instrument at each broker: symbol name, digits, contract size and even reported tick value vary, and can change over time at one broker. Anything expressed in 'points' or 'pips', and any lot-size formula, must be derived from live symbol properties.
checked.note: Core claim confirmed from primary broker documents; several supporting examples are not. CONFIRMED: Capital.com MT5 spec PDF lists 'Gold' contract 100, digits 2 and 'Silver' contract 5000, digits 3, min/step 0.01 (extracted from the PDF text). IC Markets commodity sheet shows Silver 'Contract size (MT4 Volume 1.00) 1,000 Oz', minimum '10 Oz XAG (MT4 Volume 0.01)', stops level '0 (no minimum order distance)'; the sheet is undated and MT4-labelled, as the report said. So the 5x silver contract-size difference (1,000 vs 5,000 oz) is real across two primary sources. Admirals notice confirmed: GOLD, XAUUSD-Z, XAUAUD-Z go from three to two decimals on 2 August 2025 (3320.100 -> 3320.10), with 'Check your automated strategies'. Exness three-decimal gold quote confirmed only via the secondary Myforex article (updated 2026.10.25). NOT CONFIRMED: the cited TMGM page does not show any contract size (nor does TMGM's precious-metals page), so 'TMGM lists XAG 1,000' is unsupported by its citation; IG 5,000 oz has no citation; the RoboForex digits change source returned HTTP 403; the XAUUSDm suffix was not re-checked. WEAK: the 'wrong tick value' point rests on forum users' anecdotes (one user reports getting 10 instead of 1; another recommends OrderCalcProfit); the only moderator on that page merely suggests OrderCheck and does not confirm brokers report wrong values. Treat the tick-value part as a prudent precaution, not an established fact. Search budget exhausted, so no independent search was run.

checked.claim: The built-in MQL5 economic calendar works only in a live, connected terminal: in the Strategy Tester calendar calls fail (error 4014 FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED) or return nothing, and calendar timestamps are in trade-server time, with historical events mis-shifted by an hour for the part of the year when DST state differs.
checked.note: Tried to refute by looking for a newer build that added calendar history to the tester; found none. Official MQL5 Book: 'Calendar functions cannot be used in the tester', error FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED (4014), and the developer 'must independently change the times of historical news in those periods' when DST mode differs. MQL5 reference: 'All functions for working with the economic calendar use the trade server time.' MQL5 article 22580 (28 May 2026): 'None work in the Strategy Tester because the tester has no server connection during historical replay', with a CSV export workaround. I read the official MetaTrader 5 release notes for every listed build from March 2025 through Build 6230 (24 September 2026, the newest listed): no entry mentions calendar support in the Strategy Tester; the only calendar item is the AI Assistant reading the calendar in Build 6230. The forum thread the report flagged as possibly contradicting (449652) does not: a moderator there states 'Calendar data is not available in Backtest. Only live you can request data', and the 'it works' reply only links a workaround video. Caveats: the limitation is stated in the Book and articles, not on the reference page for testing itself; and absence from release notes is not proof, so a one-line runtime check in the tester is still worthwhile. Search budget exhausted; verification was by direct fetch of primary pages.

checked.claim: Broker server time is typically GMT+2 in winter and GMT+3 in US summer time (New York-close alignment), switching on US DST dates; MQL5 offers no reliable server-UTC offset, and TimeGMT() depends on the local PC clock. Session filters built on fixed hour offsets drift by one hour during the US/EU DST mismatch weeks.
checked.note: Platform facts confirmed on primary pages; the 'typically' is a generalisation from only two brokers. CONFIRMED: IC Markets sheet: 'To align the daily chart candles with New York close (5pm ET) IC Markets server time and charts are GMT + 2 or GMT + 3 when daylight savings is in effect' (it does not say which country's DST). Pepperstone: 'Server time is set to GMT +3 while US daylight savings is in place' and GMT+2 otherwise. MQL5 docs: TimeGMT() is 'calculated taking into account the DST switch by the local time' on the computer, and 'During testing in the strategy tester, TimeGMT() is always equal to TimeTradeServer() simulated server time'; TimeTradeServer() is calculated 'in the client terminal and depends on the time settings on your computer'; the testing page says local, server and GMT time are all equal in the tester, deliberately. So a server-UTC offset computed in the tester is always zero: a hard constraint for backtesting session and news filters. FTMO update of 12 Mar 2026 confirms platform time GMT+3, Max Daily Loss monitored in Prague time, and that from 29 Mar 2026 the offset 'will again be just 1 hour'. Caveats: (1) the cited FTMO page does not contain the '8 Mar 2026' date; that is simply the US DST start date, so the 2-hour-offset window is inferred, not quoted; (2) 'no reliable server-UTC offset' is an inference: live, TimeTradeServer() minus TimeGMT() works if the PC clock is correct, it only fails in the tester; (3) GMT+2/+3 with US DST is common but not universal, so the bot must measure the offset on the actual broker rather than assume it. Search budget exhausted, so I could not search for brokers using other conventions.

checked.claim: Prop-firm rule sets differ by firm, by programme and over time; the bot needs a configurable compliance layer (daily loss anchored to the firm's clock, static vs end-of-day vs intraday trailing max loss, news execution windows that also cover SL/TP fills, best-day consistency caps, order-count limits).
checked.note: Numbers re-checked on the firms' own pages (fetched 2026-11-14). FTMO objectives: 2-Step daily loss 5% of initial capital measured from the balance at 00:00 CE(S)T, tested on equity ('Balance + Open Positions P/L ± Swaps – Commissions'); Max Loss 10% static; targets 10% then 5%; minimum 4 trading days. 1-Step: daily loss 3%, Max Loss 10% end-of-day trailing. Instant: daily loss 3%, 10% intraday balance-based trailing, best day <= 30% of total profit. All match the report. One wording correction: for orders from 12 Oct 2026 the 1-Step rule is called 'Consistency' and 'replaces the Best Day Rule' (best day <= 50% of total profit); the legacy Best Day Rule (orders before that date) is 50% of Positive Days' Profit, a different denominator. Both are 'not treated as a rule breach'. This rule change itself confirms the 'over time' part. FTMO news FAQ: execution restricted '2 minutes before and 2 minutes after', 'including your Stop Loss, Take Profit or any other pending orders'; Swing and Challenge/Verification exempt; Gold (XAUUSD) listed for USD events, XAGUSD not listed; violation 'may result in termination'. FTMO strategies FAQ: 'a limit of 200 orders at a time' and '2000 max positions per day' confirmed; the 'maximum capital allocation rule' is named but not defined. The5ers: High Stakes 2 minutes before/after, judged at trigger time, profits deducted, bracketing banned elsewhere: confirmed. FundedNext: 5 minutes before/after, 40% of profit counted, on Stellar 1-Step, 2-Step and Lite funded accounts, including SL/TP and pending orders: confirmed. NOT VERIFIED: the FundingPips figures (5 or 10 minute windows, 5-hour exemption, 35%/15% consistency) because its help centre returned HTTP 403; treat those numbers as unconfirmed. Search budget exhausted; no independent search for later rule changes was possible.

checked.claim: MQL5.com publishes no licence for the Code Base. The Terms of Use contain no Code Base clause, the Code Base is not among the documents the Terms incorporate, and there is no public Code Base rules page.
checked.note: Checked against the live pages on 2026-11-14. In the Terms of Use, "CodeBase" appears once, in the navigation bar only. Section 2.6 incorporates exactly the twelve documents the report lists; none covers the Code Base, and the definition of "MQL5 Services" does not name it either. /en/code/rules returns 404, as do /ru/code/rules, /en/code/mt5/rules and /en/code/mt4/rules. /en/about/rules exists but is a short conduct page with no licence text. /en/code/new redirects to login. The October 2025 guide (published 2025-10-09) does say "rules for formatting code and text". Limits: the same guide says the submission flow shows "two pages" of publication rules with checkboxes; neither the report nor I could read them, so the accurate wording is "no public licence found", not proof that no licence grant exists. Web search was unavailable in this run (budget exhausted), so I could only test known and guessed URLs, not search for a rules page elsewhere.

checked.claim: The Terms contain general restrictions that plausibly reach downloaded Code Base files: no reproducing or reselling site content (3.9), no removing copyright notices (3.13 IV), and no automated access by scripts or crawlers (3.7). Whether the reselling clause is meant to cover user-uploaded source code is not stated.
checked.note: All quoted clause texts match the live Terms word for word: 3.7 (automated means, scripts, crawlers), 3.9 (reproduce, duplicate, copy, sell, trade or resell; retain notices), 3.13(IV), the definition of "Content", and 11.4 (Cyprus law and courts). Two additions the report missed, both pointing the same way for design: (1) robots.txt disallows /*/code/download/*/ and /*/code/viewcode/* for all user agents, which reinforces the no-bulk-downloader conclusion; (2) section 3.7 permits use through "the interface that is provided by MetaQuotes Ltd on www.mql5.com or the MetaQuotes Software interface", and MetaQuotes publishes an official Code Base RSS feed at /en/code/rss, so the terminal, MetaEditor and the RSS feed are the sanctioned routes. Applying 3.9 to user-uploaded source files remains an interpretation, as the report itself says. Note that both the report's 40-file sample and my re-check used scripted fetches of the kind 3.7 forbids.

checked.claim: The only MetaQuotes staff position found is a 2013 admin forum post: using Code Base examples is allowed, converting their algorithms to other languages is allowed, and re-publishing the code outside mql4.com and mql5.com is forbidden. In 2015 the CEO was asked directly which licence applies and did not name one.
checked.note: The quotes are accurate. Rashid Umarov, labelled Admin, post #7 dated 2013.09.18 06:08, wrote the text as quoted, in reply to a question about porting MetaQuotes-authored MQL4 indicators to another language for a commercial project. In the 2015 thread "Code Base licences" (66 posts, 7 pages, all fetched), the only staff-labelled post is Renat Fatkhullin, labelled Admin, #12 on 2015.11.02: "The topikstarter asked the wrong question in his head." No licence was named. What the report left out weakens the 2013 post as a basis for design: in the same thread, post #9 (2013.09.19), the asker says a follow-up email to MetaQuotes was answered by pointing him to the MQL5 Terms of Use, which he read as a refusal, and he gave up. That is second-hand, but it is a second reported MetaQuotes response that conflicts with the admin's permissive answer. Not verified: that this is the "only" staff position (search was unavailable, so I could not look for others), and Fatkhullin's CEO title, which the page does not show.

checked.claim: Explicit open-source licences inside Code Base files appear to be rare. In a 40-file sample (20 newest entries, 20 top-rated MT5 Experts), 38 of 40 had a #property copyright line and 0 of 40 carried MIT, GPL, BSD, Apache, Creative Commons text or "All rights reserved"; the copyright line is often a template default.
checked.note: I recounted the report's working files: 40 source files, 38 with #property copyright, 0 with any licence text or "all rights reserved", three naming "MetaQuotes Ltd." and three reading "Your Name". The entry IDs match the live Code Base listing and the top-rated Experts page. Entry 68125's description does say "Feel free to use, modify, and learn from this code". Independent re-sample of 12 files not in the original set (6 newest entries, 79522 to 79530, and 6 top-rated MT5 libraries): 0 of 12 with licence text, 9 of 12 with a copyright line, and no permission wording in the 12 descriptions. The ALGLIB exception is real and stronger than reported: besides the page text "It can be used for free under GPL 2+", the downloaded file diffequations.mqh carries a GNU GPL version 2 or later notice in its header. Limits: only one file per entry was checked, the samples are small and not random, and MT4 and older entries were not tested, so "rare" is a reasonable working assumption and not a measured rate.

checked.claim: Market mechanics add practical risk for derived products: only compiled EX5/EX4 files are allowed, which conflicts with copyleft licences; look-alike products (same idea, differing only in inputs, symbols or timeframes) are treated as spam; and products can be removed without explanation, including for similarity to another product.
checked.note: The three rule texts match the live Market Rules word for word: section IV compiled-only; section IV multiple copies "based on the same idea and differ only in input parameter settings, symbols, and/or timeframes", with removal of all copies and a ban from all paid MQL5.com services; section I removal "without any explanation". So a gold EA and a silver EA that differ only in symbol and settings fall squarely inside the spam rule; ship one multi-symbol product. The MetaQuotes post of 2018.09.07 confirms Code Base and Market publication moved to automated checks. The May 2026 seller post exists (2026.05.25) but is one unverified account, and by the seller's own telling the support reply addressed the product description, not the code. The copyleft conflict is a legal inference, not a MetaQuotes statement, but it is sound: the ALGLIB files carry a GPL 2+ header and the Market accepts no source. Also relevant to design and not in the claim: the same section bans any DLL calls and third-party licence-control or WebRequest-based sales systems in Market products. No documentation of how similarity is detected was found.

checked.claim: The general legal baseline matches the cautious reading: software copyright arises automatically and protects the code as written, not the trading idea or algorithm. Translating or adapting code is itself a restricted act, so a line-by-line port to another language is not a re-implementation.
checked.note: Primary texts confirmed word for word: TRIPS Article 9(2) and 10(1) on the WTO site; Directive 2009/24/EC Article 1(2) and Article 4(1)(b) ("translation, adaptation, arrangement and any other alteration") on legislation.gov.uk; the choosealicense.com sentence, which reads "that generally means you have no permission". The SAS Institute v World Programming holding (C-406/10, 2 May 2012) I could confirm only through Wikipedia; EUR-Lex returned an empty page and the Court's site needs JavaScript, so the judgment text itself was not read. Three caveats for design. (1) As I recall the judgment (not re-read here), World Programming had no access to SAS source code and copied behaviour by observation, and the Court said building similar elements with the aid of the source code could be partial reproduction. Reading an EA's source, writing a spec and re-coding is therefore less protected than that case; the idea/expression rule supports it, SAS does not directly bless it. (2) The Cyprus clause governs the contract with MetaQuotes; a dispute with a Code Base author would turn on the copyright law of the country where protection is claimed. (3) The claim sits in tension with the 2013 admin post saying algorithms may be converted to other languages; that post concerned MetaQuotes' own indicators and cannot grant rights in other authors' code.

findings.claim: Diversified, slow (1-12 month) time-series momentum / trend following is the only family here with long, multi-source, cost-inclusive evidence - but its performance decayed sharply after 2009 (roughly when it was popularised), and it is cyclical with deep multi-year drawdowns.

On a single instrument (gold or silver alone) trend following is NOT a statistically established edge; most of the published 'alpha' comes from diversification across dozens of markets and from volatility scaling.

Transaction-cost sensitivity splits the families cleanly: slow trend is almost cost-immune in futures terms, while every documented intraday gold effect has a gross edge of only a few basis points per trade - the same order as round-trip costs.
Classic technical trading rules (moving-average crossovers, channel breakouts, etc.) on commodities and intraday gold/silver mostly fail once data snooping is controlled; silver is worse than gold.

Intraday momentum (rest-of-day return predicting the last 30 minutes) is statistically real in gold and stronger in silver, but economically tiny, measured gross of costs, and tied to a session definition that no longer matches the 23-hour electronic market.

Opening-range, London-session and New-York-session breakouts on gold are folklore as far as published evidence goes: I found no peer-reviewed, cost-inclusive test on gold; what exists is vendor backtests. The academic ORB evidence is on crude oil and US equities, and an independent replication on index CFDs found the edge is consumed by costs.

The gold overnight / Asian-hours drift is a genuinely documented anomaly (positive returns outside Western trading hours, flat-to-negative returns during them), but it has weakened, its 'fixing-time sell-off' component was regime-specific (about 2007-2012), and it is marginal to untradable after realistic costs.

Short-horizon mean reversion (fade the big day, RSI-style pullback buying) has no credible cost-surviving evidence on gold or silver; the limited evidence points the other way (continuation after large moves).

Gold-silver ratio pairs trading rests on a cointegration relationship that is unstable and regime-dependent; the mean-reversion trade has worked in windows and then failed violently, most recently in 2020 and 2025-26.

Volatility targeting and ATR-based sizing are risk-control tools, not sources of edge, for gold and silver: they do not raise the Sharpe ratio in commodities but they do reduce tail risk and stabilise risk exposure.
Grid, martingale and averaging-down systems have no edge of their own and a documented path to ruin: they trade a high win rate for a rare account-sized loss, and leverage is the mechanism.

The base rate for retail leveraged trading is that roughly 70-90% of accounts lose money, persistence does not help, and there is no evidence of learning - this is the prior any retail gold/silver bot should be judged against.

There are no credible population-level statistics on how retail expert advisors perform over time; the nearest evidence (copy-trading studies, prop-firm data, SEBI's algo split) says followers earn no abnormal return after costs and that algorithmic profits accrue to institutions, not retail.

Recent gold-only backtests (roughly 2015-2026) are contaminated by one of the strongest gold bull markets on record, so long-biased or breakout rules look far better than they are; headline claims from this window should be discounted unless they beat buy-and-hold and work symmetrically long and short.

findings.claim: MT5 tick modes differ materially in realism. 'Every tick based on real ticks' replays the broker's recorded Bid/Ask ticks (variable spread inside a minute) and is the only mode MetaQuotes calls 'as close to real conditions as possible'. 'Every tick' synthesises ticks from M1 bars. '1 minute OHLC' and 'Open prices only' fill pending orders, SL and TP at the requested price, which is optimistic. If real ticks are missing, the tester falls back to generated ticks without stopping the run.

Spread in the MT5 tester is not modelled; it is read from history. With generated ticks there is one fixed spread per M1 bar, and community testing indicates the stored M1 spread is the minute's minimum, so generated-tick and OHLC backtests probably understate real spread cost. This matters most for gold and silver around news and the daily rollover.

MT5 cost and execution modelling is partial. Commission is configurable in the tester. Execution delay can be zero, fixed (for example measured ping) or random. Swaps appear to use today's symbol specification for the whole history. Delays do not apply to pending, SL or TP triggering. Liquidity, partial fills and real slippage on market orders are not modelled.

MT5's built-in 'Forward' option is a single in-sample/out-of-sample split, not walk-forward analysis. Rolling or anchored walk-forward has to be automated separately. The usual pass marks (walk-forward efficiency of at least 50%, more than half of out-of-sample windows profitable) are conventions, and one peer-reviewed comparison found walk-forward the weakest method at preventing false discoveries.

A custom OnTester criterion ('Custom max') lets the optimiser rank passes on a robustness-oriented score, but no criterion removes selection bias. MetaQuotes' own built-in 'Complex Criterion max' has no published formula, and MetaQuotes' book example shows most top in-sample passes failing in the forward period.

The number of configurations tried must be counted and bounded against data length. With 5 years of data, no more than about 45 independent configurations should be tried before a zero-skill strategy is expected to show an in-sample annualised Sharpe of 1. A typical MT5 optimisation with thousands of passes far exceeds this.

The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is the standard correction for selection among many trials plus non-normal returns. The pass level used in the source paper is DSR of at least 0.95. Even an annualised Sharpe of 2.5 over 5 years of daily data fails once about 100 independent trials are accounted for.

The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO), estimated by combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV), measures how often the in-sample best configuration ranks below the median out of sample. The authors' customary rejection level is PBO above 0.05, with S=16 partitions suggested. The same paper explains why a single hold-out is weak evidence.

Minimum trade counts (30, 100, 200+) and 'N years of data' rules are conventions without a primary statistical source. The defensible quantities are the Sharpe ratio's standard error and the resulting t-statistic, which show that short backtests and short forward tests carry little statistical information.

Monte Carlo trade resampling (shuffling order, or bootstrap with replacement) is a tool for sizing drawdown risk, not for detecting overfitting. It assumes trades are independent, and every threshold attached to it is a convention.

Choosing a parameter set from a broad plateau rather than an isolated peak is sound practice, but it has no formal threshold. The closest published method is Walton's System Parameter Permutation, which takes the median result across all tested parameter combinations as the realistic expectation.

Gold and silver backtests are broker-specific. Spot metals are over-the-counter with no single price, the MT5 tester only uses the connected broker's own M1 and tick history, and real-tick depth varies by broker. A result on one broker's data is one sample, and cross-feed testing needs custom symbols or accounts at other brokers.

Known tester pitfalls: the MQL5 economic calendar is only available online, not in the tester; TimeGMT() in the tester equals server time, so GMT-offset and session logic silently break; broker server time usually switches between GMT+2 and GMT+3 on the US daylight-saving schedule; bars of different symbols are not synchronised; and WebRequest and alerts do not run in the tester.

No authoritative source sets a demo or forward-test duration. The principled measure is the Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL), which implies that a 1-3 month demo cannot statistically confirm an edge unless the Sharpe ratio is very high. Demo runs mainly test implementation and execution parity; practitioner 'incubation' of 3-12 months is convention.

The N=10 -> 1.57, '7 independent configurations for a 2-year backtest' and 'necessary, non-sufficient condition' quotes are also present. I recomputed the formula: N=45 gives 4.998 years, N=10 gives E[max]=1.575, N=1,000 gives 10.6 years, N=10,000 gives 14.9 years, so the report's extrapolations are correct. Caveats, none of which refute it: (1) the 45 figure comes from the approximation formula, not the looser bound 2ln(N) that the report's evidence line shows (that bound would give 7.6 years at N=45); (2) the bound is tied to a target in-sample Sharpe of 1 and scales with 1/Sharpe^2; (3) it assumes independent trials, and the paper itself calls this 'quite conservative' for correlated trials, so raw MT5 pass counts overstate N. WebSearch was unavailable (session search budget exhausted), so I could not look for published critiques; the check is against the primary source only.

fact_check.claim: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR) is the standard correction for selection among many trials plus non-normal returns. The pass level used in the source paper is DSR of at least 0.95. Even an annualised Sharpe of 2.5 over 5 years of daily data fails once about 100 independent trials are accounted for.
fact_check.note: Read the paper PDF (Bailey and Lopez de Prado, 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio', version 31 July 2014, marked 'Journal of Portfolio Management, Forthcoming, 2014'). The worked example (annualised SR 2.5, 'a daily sample of 5 years', T=1250) is rejected 'at a 95% confidence level'; 'only a 90% chance that the true SR ... is greater than zero'; at N=46 the DSR 'would have been 0.9505'; with Normal returns the same level is reached at N=88. The symbols for the inputs are lost in text extraction, so I recomputed: with N=100, trial-Sharpe variance 1/2 (annualised), skew -3, kurtosis 10, 250 observations per year, DSR = 0.9004; N=46 gives 0.9505; Normal returns with N=88 give 0.9505. All three match the paper, so the inputs the report quoted 'from recollection' are right. Caveats: (1) the failure at about 100 trials is conditional on those inputs, especially the variance of Sharpe across trials (1/2) and the negative skew; with Normal returns DSR at N=100 is 0.943, a narrow fail, and a smaller cross-trial variance would pass. It is one worked example, not a general rule. (2) 0.95 is the confidence level used in the example, not a formally prescribed pass mark. (3) 'the standard correction' is the report's characterisation; I found no source that establishes it as a standard, and could not search for one (search budget exhausted). The Harvey quotes ('only a rule of thumb', 'a serious mistake' on the 50% haircut) are confirmed on the Man Group page.

fact_check.claim: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO), estimated by combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV), measures how often the in-sample best configuration ranks below the median out of sample. The authors' customary rejection level is PBO above 0.05, with S=16 partitions suggested. The same paper explains why a single hold-out is weak evidence.
fact_check.note: Read the paper PDF (Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, Zhu, revised February 2015). Verbatim: 'a customary approach would be to reject models for which PBO is estimated to be greater than 0.05'; 'we believe that S = 16 is a reasonable value to use in most cases'; 'N >> 10 is required'; hold-out 'should not be applied to an analysis with less than 1,000 observations'; 'Different hold-outs are thus likely to lead to different conclusions'; 'Hiding trials will lead to an underestimation of the overfit'; 'incorrect transaction costs'; 'PBO should not be the objective function'. The MQL5 article (Njoroge, 13 March 2026) does say values 'such as 0.1 or 0.2 are informal rules of thumb'. Two corrections that matter for design: (1) the '12,780 combinations' figure is the paper's own number but is a transposition error; C(16,8) = 12,870. (2) The report omits a limitation stated in section 5.2: for guided searches (which is what MT5 genetic optimisation is), the columns of the trial matrix 'should be the final outcome of each guided search ... and not the intermediate steps'. Feeding every genetic pass into CSCV, as the report's implications suggest ('export all passes'), is not what the paper prescribes; a complete grid search fits the method, a genetic run does not without that adjustment. Also the S=16 rationale is tied to about 4 years of daily data (quarterly blocks). No independent critique search was possible (search budget exhausted).

fact_check.claim: Spread in the MT5 tester is not modelled; it is read from history. With generated ticks there is one fixed spread per M1 bar, and community testing indicates the stored M1 spread is the minute's minimum, so generated-tick and OHLC backtests probably understate real spread cost. This matters most for gold and silver around news and the daily rollover.
fact_check.note: Documented part confirmed on MetaQuotes pages: 'During testing, the spread is not modeled but is taken from historical data'; 'the spread is always considered floating'; 'The Ask price is calculated as Bid + fixed spread of a corresponding minute bar'; zero or negative spread falls back to the last known spread; with real ticks 'a spread may change within a minute bar'. The 'minimum of the minute' part is weaker than the report says. (1) The MqlRates documentation defines the field only as 'Spread'. (2) Thread 438312 has forum moderators stating it is the minimum (Verleyen quoted from 2018; Carreiro in 2022: 'No official information is provided by MetaQuotes ... the consensus is that it is the minimum'). (3) Thread 17858, page 2, has the same moderator saying the opposite in 2014: 'The spread registered with M1 data, is the higher value of the spread during the minute.' (4) Neither cited thread contains the statement the report attributes to a MetaQuotes developer about a change from maximum to minimum; that attribution is unverified. So 'understates spread' is plausible but rests on conflicting forum statements, and the report already notes some brokers leave the field empty. Additional point the report misses: MT5 release notes for build 6060 (23 July 2026) say 'Fixed the application of custom spreads in the "Open prices only" testing mode', which indicates the tester accepts a custom spread override, so history is the default source, not the only one, and a widened-spread stress run is possible in the tester. The help page I read does not describe that setting, so check it in the terminal. Adjacent finding from the same pages (report claims 1 and 3): the quote 'Limit orders are executed at the price specified in the order (without a slippage)' applies to exchange instruments. For non-exchange instruments, which is how spot gold and silver CFDs are normally configured, the page says triggering of all pending orders and SL/TP 'is performed by Bid and Ask prices' and 'Execution is performed by the current Bid and Ask market prices at the moment of triggering'; only in 'Open prices only' and '1 minute OHLC' modes are they filled at the order price. The gold/silver news and rollover link is the report's inference and was not checked. No web search was possible (budget exhausted); checks were direct fetches.

fact_check.claim: MT5's built-in 'Forward' option is a single in-sample/out-of-sample split, not walk-forward analysis. Rolling or anchored walk-forward has to be automated separately. The usual pass marks (walk-forward efficiency of at least 50%, more than half of out-of-sample windows profitable) are conventions, and one peer-reviewed comparison found walk-forward the weakest method at preventing false discoveries.
fact_check.note: MT5 part confirmed on the MetaQuotes help page: Forward options are No, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, Custom; 'The second (latest) part of the total period is always taken for the forward testing'; '10% (in the full search) or 25% (in the genetic algorithm) of best runs are selected and then tested on the forward period'; a floor of 256 runs. That is one split. MQL5 article 3279 (Korotky, 15 September 2017) confirms the built-in tester 'does not allow launching it at the touch of a button', describes rolling, anchored and cluster walk-forward, and says 'It is recommended to have a consistency above 50%'. That is one article author's recommendation, which fits 'convention'. Not verified: (1) the Arian, Norouzi Mobarekeh and Seco paper exists as described (Knowledge-Based Systems, vol. 305, article 112477, 2024, confirmed through Crossref and OpenAlex), but I could not retrieve its abstract or text: SSRN and ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403, the Scribd copy did not load, and OpenAlex holds no abstract. The quoted phrase 'notable shortcomings in false discovery prevention' is therefore unconfirmed in this check. Even taken at face value it does not say 'the weakest method'; that is the report's stronger wording. The study is also a synthetic controlled environment with machine-learning strategies, so applying it to a rule-based metals EA is an extrapolation. (2) The 50% walk-forward-efficiency rule attributed to Pardo was not checked against the book (the report says the same). (3) MQL5 article 23250 was not read. Search budget was exhausted, so no independent search for counter-evidence was run.

fact_check.claim: Known tester pitfalls: the MQL5 economic calendar is only available online, not in the tester; TimeGMT() in the tester equals server time, so GMT-offset and session logic silently break; broker server time usually switches between GMT+2 and GMT+3 on the US daylight-saving schedule; bars of different symbols are not synchronised; and WebRequest and alerts do not run in the tester.
fact_check.note: Each element checked against a MetaQuotes or broker page. Calendar: the MQL5 Book says 'The calendar is available for MQL programs only online' and gives the cache-file workaround with #property tester_file, plus the one-hour correction for events from the opposite daylight-saving half-year. I read the MT5 release notes for every listed build from 5430 (13 November 2025) to 6230 (24 September 2026, the newest shown): none adds calendar support to the Strategy Tester. Build 6230's calendar item is for the AI Assistant, not the tester. TimeGMT: the function page says 'During testing in the strategy tester, TimeGMT() is always equal to TimeTradeServer() simulated server time', and the testing page says TimeLocal() equals TimeTradeServer() in the tester. Calendar functions 'use the trade server time'. Not executed in the tester: Alert, MessageBox, PlaySound, SendFTP, SendMail, SendNotification, WebRequest. Multi-symbol: 'a new bar for each symbol is opened, regardless of how the bar opened on another symbol'. Weakest element: 'usually GMT+2/GMT+3 on the US schedule' is confirmed only for Darwinex ('Time in Metatrader terminals is set to New York Close', GMT+3 in US summertime, otherwise GMT+2). It is a common convention, not a platform rule, so the offset must be confirmed for the actual broker. The calendar statement comes from the MQL5 Book, not from the calendar reference page, which is silent on tester behaviour. Related tester changes worth knowing: build 6060 (23 July 2026) lists 'Fixed percentage-based swap calculations' and a custom-spread fix in 'Open prices only' mode, so results from older builds may differ. Search budget was exhausted, so I could not search forums for reports of calendar functions working in newer tester builds.

open_questions: How far back does the target broker's real-tick history go for XAUUSD and XAGUSD, and how does its recorded spread compare with live spread at rollover and around major news? This can only be answered by a tick audit on the actual account.

What exactly does the MT5 M1 bar 'spread' field store (minimum, open or last of the minute) on current builds and at the target broker? MetaQuotes has not documented it; the 'minimum' reading is community evidence.

Does the tester apply only the current swap specification to all history on current builds, and how does it handle the triple-swap day and percentage-mode swaps for metals? No official statement was found.

Has any 2026 MT5 build added economic-calendar support in the Strategy Tester? The MQL5 Book says the calendar is online-only and the release notes I saw do not mention a change, but I did not review every build.

How should the effective number of independent trials be estimated for MT5 genetic optimisations, where passes are highly correlated? The DSR paper offers an average-correlation method, but it needs per-pass return series, which the standard XML export does not include.
How does MT5 compute its reported Sharpe ratio (sampling period and annualisation)? It may not be directly usable as the per-observation Sharpe that DSR and MinTRL require.
Pardo's 50% walk-forward-efficiency threshold and Chan's '252 observations per free parameter' rule were found only in secondary sources; the original book wording was not verified.

The DSR worked-example inputs (N=100, trial-Sharpe variance 1/2, skew -3, kurtosis 10) were not legible in my text extraction of the paper and are quoted from recollection; T=1250, the 0.9505 result at N=46 and the '90% chance' statement were read directly.
What is the live slippage and requote distribution for market and stop orders in gold at the target broker? Neither the tester nor a demo account measures it; only small-size live trading will.

Is PBO at or below 0.05 achievable for a small retail parameter grid, given that the method needs many trials (N much greater than 10) and at least a few years of data for S=16 partitions? It may be too strict or too noisy at this scale.

findings.claim: MQL5.com publishes no licence for the Code Base. The Terms of Use contain no Code Base clause, the Code Base is not among the documents the Terms incorporate, and there is no public Code Base rules page.
Copyright stays with each author. The only licence the Terms create runs from the uploader to MetaQuotes, for running the website; nothing is granted to people who download.

The Terms contain general restrictions that plausibly reach downloaded Code Base files: no reproducing or reselling site content, no removing copyright notices, and no automated access. Whether the reselling clause is meant to cover user-uploaded source code is not stated.

MetaQuotes' own Code Base pages invite users to download, run, study and build their own programs on the published code. That supports personal use and adaptation as the intended purpose, but it is site copy, not a licence, and it says nothing about redistribution or sale.

The only MetaQuotes staff position I found is a 2013 admin forum post: using Code Base examples is allowed, converting their algorithms to other languages is allowed, and re-publishing the code outside mql4.com and mql5.com is forbidden. In 2015 the CEO was asked directly which licence applies and did not name one.

On its newer Git platform, MQL5 Algo Forge, MetaQuotes states the default explicitly: no licence file means all rights reserved, and the author keeps full copyright. This is the clearest indication of how MetaQuotes itself treats unlicensed public code, though the document covers Forge, not the Code Base.

Explicit open-source licences inside Code Base files appear to be rare. In a 40-file sample, none carried MIT, GPL, BSD, Apache or Creative Commons text; almost all carried only a one-line copyright property, which is often a template default.

Forum moderators and senior users in 2023 to 2025 give consistent guidance: unlicensed Code Base code is all rights reserved, commercial use or Market sale needs the author's permission, and writing new code from the same idea needs no permission. This is community guidance, not MetaQuotes policy, and looser views are also voiced.

No Market rule names the Code Base, but the Market Developer Distribution Agreement requires the seller to hold the copyright or have distribution rights in any third-party material, and attaches takedown, refund and indemnity consequences to infringement.

Market mechanics add practical risk for derived products: only compiled files are allowed, which conflicts with copyleft licences; look-alike products are treated as spam; and products can be removed without explanation, including for similarity to another product.

The general legal baseline matches the cautious reading: software copyright arises automatically and protects the code as written, not the trading idea or algorithm. Translating or adapting code is itself a restricted act, so a line-by-line port to another language is not a re-implementation.
The Code Base has attribution mechanics but no licence field, and it is treated more loosely than MQL5 Articles, which carry an explicit all-rights-reserved notice.

If the bot is built or extended through MQL5 Freelance, the default rule gives the customer all exclusive rights, which a developer cannot honestly deliver for any part copied from unlicensed Code Base code.

fact_check.claim: MQL5.com publishes no licence for the Code Base. The Terms of Use contain no Code Base clause, the Code Base is not among the documents the Terms incorporate, and there is no public Code Base rules page.
fact_check.note: Checked against the live pages on 2026-11-14. In the Terms of Use, "CodeBase" appears once, in the navigation bar only. Section 2.6 incorporates exactly the twelve documents the report lists; none covers the Code Base, and the definition of "MQL5 Services" does not name it either. /en/code/rules returns 404, as do /ru/code/rules, /en/code/mt5/rules and /en/code/mt4/rules. /en/about/rules exists but is a short conduct page with no licence text. /en/code/new redirects to login. The October 2025 guide (published 2025-10-09) does say "rules for formatting code and text". Limits: the same guide says the submission flow shows "two pages" of publication rules with checkboxes; neither the report nor I could read them, so the accurate wording is "no public licence found", not proof that no licence grant exists. Web search was unavailable in this run (budget exhausted), so I could only test known and guessed URLs, not search for a rules page elsewhere.

fact_check.claim: The Terms contain general restrictions that plausibly reach downloaded Code Base files: no reproducing or reselling site content (3.9), no removing copyright notices (3.13 IV), and no automated access by scripts or crawlers (3.7). Whether the reselling clause is meant to cover user-uploaded source code is not stated.
fact_check.note: All quoted clause texts match the live Terms word for word: 3.7 (automated means, scripts, crawlers), 3.9 (reproduce, duplicate, copy, sell, trade or resell; retain notices), 3.13(IV), the definition of "Content", and 11.4 (Cyprus law and courts). Two additions the report missed, both pointing the same way for design: (1) robots.txt disallows /*/code/download/*/ and /*/code/viewcode/* for all user agents, which reinforces the no-bulk-downloader conclusion; (2) section 3.7 permits use through "the interface that is provided by MetaQuotes Ltd on www.mql5.com or the MetaQuotes Software interface", and MetaQuotes publishes an official Code Base RSS feed at /en/code/rss, so the terminal, MetaEditor and the RSS feed are the sanctioned routes. Applying 3.9 to user-uploaded source files remains an interpretation, as the report itself says. Note that both the report's 40-file sample and my re-check used scripted fetches of the kind 3.7 forbids.

fact_check.claim: The only MetaQuotes staff position found is a 2013 admin forum post: using Code Base examples is allowed, converting their algorithms to other languages is allowed, and re-publishing the code outside mql4.com and mql5.com is forbidden. In 2015 the CEO was asked directly which licence applies and did not name one.
fact_check.note: The quotes are accurate. Rashid Umarov, labelled Admin, post #7 dated 2013.09.18 06:08, wrote the text as quoted, in reply to a question about porting MetaQuotes-authored MQL4 indicators to another language for a commercial project. In the 2015 thread "Code Base licences" (66 posts, 7 pages, all fetched), the only staff-labelled post is Renat Fatkhullin, labelled Admin, #12 on 2015.11.02: "The topikstarter asked the wrong question in his head." No licence was named. What the report left out weakens the 2013 post as a basis for design: in the same thread, post #9 (2013.09.19), the asker says a follow-up email to MetaQuotes was answered by pointing him to the MQL5 Terms of Use, which he read as a refusal, and he gave up. That is second-hand, but it is a second reported MetaQuotes response that conflicts with the admin's permissive answer. Not verified: that this is the "only" staff position (search was unavailable, so I could not look for others), and Fatkhullin's CEO title, which the page does not show.

fact_check.claim: Explicit open-source licences inside Code Base files appear to be rare. In a 40-file sample (20 newest entries, 20 top-rated MT5 Experts), 38 of 40 had a #property copyright line and 0 of 40 carried MIT, GPL, BSD, Apache, Creative Commons text or "All rights reserved"; the copyright line is often a template default.
fact_check.note: I recounted the report's working files: 40 source files, 38 with #property copyright, 0 with any licence text or "all rights reserved", three naming "MetaQuotes Ltd." and three reading "Your Name". The entry IDs match the live Code Base listing and the top-rated Experts page. Entry 68125's description does say "Feel free to use, modify, and learn from this code". Independent re-sample of 12 files not in the original set (6 newest entries, 79522 to 79530, and 6 top-rated MT5 libraries): 0 of 12 with licence text, 9 of 12 with a copyright line, and no permission wording in the 12 descriptions. The ALGLIB exception is real and stronger than reported: besides the page text "It can be used for free under GPL 2+", the downloaded file diffequations.mqh carries a GNU GPL version 2 or later notice in its header. Limits: only one file per entry was checked, the samples are small and not random, and MT4 and older entries were not tested, so "rare" is a reasonable working assumption and not a measured rate.

fact_check.claim: Market mechanics add practical risk for derived products: only compiled EX5/EX4 files are allowed, which conflicts with copyleft licences; look-alike products (same idea, differing only in inputs, symbols or timeframes) are treated as spam; and products can be removed without explanation, including for similarity to another product.
fact_check.note: The three rule texts match the live Market Rules word for word: section IV compiled-only; section IV multiple copies "based on the same idea and differ only in input parameter settings, symbols, and/or timeframes", with removal of all copies and a ban from all paid MQL5.com services; section I removal "without any explanation". So a gold EA and a silver EA that differ only in symbol and settings fall squarely inside the spam rule; ship one multi-symbol product. The MetaQuotes post of 2018.09.07 confirms Code Base and Market publication moved to automated checks. The May 2026 seller post exists (2026.05.25) but is one unverified account, and by the seller's own telling the support reply addressed the product description, not the code. The copyleft conflict is a legal inference, not a MetaQuotes statement, but it is sound: the ALGLIB files carry a GPL 2+ header and the Market accepts no source. Also relevant to design and not in the claim: the same section bans any DLL calls and third-party licence-control or WebRequest-based sales systems in Market products. No documentation of how similarity is detected was found.

fact_check.claim: The general legal baseline matches the cautious reading: software copyright arises automatically and protects the code as written, not the trading idea or algorithm. Translating or adapting code is itself a restricted act, so a line-by-line port to another language is not a re-implementation.
fact_check.note: Primary texts confirmed word for word: TRIPS Article 9(2) and 10(1) on the WTO site; Directive 2009/24/EC Article 1(2) and Article 4(1)(b) ("translation, adaptation, arrangement and any other alteration") on legislation.gov.uk; the choosealicense.com sentence, which reads "that generally means you have no permission". The SAS Institute v World Programming holding (C-406/10, 2 May 2012) I could confirm only through Wikipedia; EUR-Lex returned an empty page and the Court's site needs JavaScript, so the judgment text itself was not read. Three caveats for design. (1) As I recall the judgment (not re-read here), World Programming had no access to SAS source code and copied behaviour by observation, and the Court said building similar elements with the aid of the source code could be partial reproduction. Reading an EA's source, writing a spec and re-coding is therefore less protected than that case; the idea/expression rule supports it, SAS does not directly bless it. (2) The Cyprus clause governs the contract with MetaQuotes; a dispute with a Code Base author would turn on the copyright law of the country where protection is claimed. (3) The claim sits in tension with the 2013 admin post saying algorithms may be converted to other languages; that post concerned MetaQuotes' own indicators and cannot grant rights in other authors' code.

open_questions: What exactly do the Code Base 'publication rules' shown in the submission form say? They sit behind login and I could not read them. They are described as formatting rules, but they could contain an originality statement or a licence grant that would change the picture.

Does MetaQuotes still hold the position its admin posted in 2013 (use allowed, re-publishing outside mql4.com and mql5.com forbidden)? I found no current official statement; a Service Desk ticket asking the question directly would be the way to settle it.

Is section 3.9 of the Terms ('will not reproduce, duplicate, copy, sell, trade or resell the content of the website') intended to cover user-uploaded Code Base source files, or only MetaQuotes' own site content? The text does not say.

Would a court recognise an implied licence for personal use and adaptation from the act of publishing in a free code library plus MetaQuotes' invitation to 'develop your own automated trading applications based on the provided codes'? This depends on jurisdiction (Cyprus law governs the Terms; the law of the place where the bot is distributed also matters) and needs a qualified lawyer.

How common are explicit licences across the whole Code Base? My sample was 40 recent and top-rated MQL5 files; older MQL4 entries and libraries may differ, and a larger count was not attempted because the Terms prohibit automated access.
How does the Market detect 'similarity' or plagiarism, and does it compare uploads against Code Base code? I found only seller anecdotes and the 2018 announcement that checks are automated.

Where is the line between a clean re-implementation and an adaptation when the logic is simple (for example a moving-average cross with an ATR stop) and independent code naturally looks alike? This is fact-specific and not answered by any source found.

What licence governs the source code shipped inside the MetaTrader 5 terminal (Standard Library, bundled ALGLIB, example EAs) when it is compiled into a product for sale? I did not review the MetaTrader end-user licence in this pass.

findings.claim: Order filling policy must be chosen at runtime from SYMBOL_FILLING_MODE plus SYMBOL_TRADE_EXEMODE; hard-coding FOK, IOC or RETURN will be rejected on some brokers (retcode 10030 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_FILL).

SL/TP and pending-order prices must respect SYMBOL_TRADE_STOPS_LEVEL and SYMBOL_TRADE_FREEZE_LEVEL (measured against the correct side of the spread), and volumes must be normalised to min/step/max and SYMBOL_VOLUME_LIMIT; a stops level of 0 does not guarantee that any distance is accepted.

The same metal is a different instrument at each broker: symbol name, digits, contract size and even reported tick value vary, and can change over time at one broker. Anything expressed in 'points' or 'pips', and any lot-size formula, must be derived from live symbol properties.

Netting and hedging accounts need different position logic: in netting there is one position per symbol and a new order's SL/TP overwrite the old ones; in hedging every close/modify must carry the position ticket, and FIFO or no-hedge account flags can reject requests.

OrderSend() returning true is not execution; the EA must branch on MqlTradeResult.retcode. Requotes belong to Instant Execution; in Market Execution the price and deviation fields are not required, so the 'slippage' parameter is not a protection there.

Around the daily rollover (5 pm New York = about 00:00 server time on GMT+2/+3 brokers) metals trading is briefly halted and spreads widen; stops are not guaranteed and fill at the next available price. News releases have a swift, significant effect on gold and silver volatility.
Margin on metals is not constant: brokers raise it by schedule (rollover, weekend, news windows) and by announcement during volatile periods, and silver generally carries stricter margin than gold.
Triple swap for spot metals is normally charged on the Wednesday-to-Thursday rollover, but the day is a per-symbol server setting that the EA can and should read instead of assuming.

Broker server time is typically GMT+2 in winter and GMT+3 in US summer time (New York-close alignment), switching on US DST dates; MQL5 offers no reliable server-UTC offset, and TimeGMT() depends on the local PC clock. Session filters built on fixed hour offsets drift by one hour during the US/EU DST mismatch weeks.

The built-in MQL5 economic calendar works only in a live, connected terminal: in the Strategy Tester calendar calls fail (error 4014 FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED) or return nothing, and calendar timestamps are in trade-server time, with historical events mis-shifted by an hour for the part of the year when DST state differs.

An EA can be re-initialised at any time (terminal restart, account re-authorisation, chart/template change) and trade events are asynchronous and unordered, so in-memory state cannot be trusted; state must be rebuilt from server-side positions/orders/history and a small persisted store.

VPS hosting reduces network latency but does not remove price slippage at news or rollover, and MetaQuotes' built-in VPS has functional limits (no DLLs, no scripts, EA-less charts ignored, one-way sync).

Prop-firm rule sets differ by firm, by programme and over time; the bot needs a configurable compliance layer (daily loss anchored to the firm's clock, static vs end-of-day vs intraday trailing max loss, news execution windows that also cover SL/TP fills, best-day consistency caps, order-count limits).

Swap-free (Islamic) accounts replace swaps on metals with flat holding/admin fees after a grace period, and the terms vary widely by broker; for multi-day holds the fee can exceed the swap it replaces and is not visible in SYMBOL_SWAP_LONG/SHORT.

fact_check.claim: Order filling policy must be chosen at runtime from SYMBOL_FILLING_MODE plus SYMBOL_TRADE_EXEMODE; hard-coding FOK, IOC or RETURN will be rejected on some brokers (retcode 10030 TRADE_RETCODE_INVALID_FILL).
fact_check.note: Re-read the MQL5 reference pages directly. Confirmed: SYMBOL_FILLING_FOK=1, IOC=2, BOC=4; the per-execution-mode table reads exactly as reported (Instant/Request: FOK and IOC 'regardless of a symbol setting', RETURN 'always'; Market: FOK/IOC 'set in the symbol settings', RETURN 'disabled regardless of the symbol settings'; Exchange: FOK/IOC per symbol, RETURN always). The docs also state 'Return orders are not allowed in the Market Execution mode' and that pending orders should use ORDER_FILLING_RETURN 'regardless of an execution type'. Retcode 10030 = 'Invalid order filling type' and 10010 = 'Only part of the request was completed' confirmed. The MQL5 Book confirms the execution mode 'is predetermined by the broker for each symbol'. Could not refute. Caveats: (1) no public per-broker table of filling flags exists, so which case applies on the user's gold/silver symbol is still unknown until read live; (2) the docs do not cover the edge case where the symbol's filling flags read as 0, so the selector should have a defined fallback. Method note: the web-search budget for this run was exhausted, so this check used direct fetches of primary documentation rather than independent searches.

fact_check.claim: OrderSend() returning true is not execution; the EA must branch on MqlTradeResult.retcode. Requotes belong to Instant Execution; in Market Execution the price and deviation fields are not required, so the 'slippage' parameter is not a protection there.
fact_check.note: Confirmed on primary pages. OrderSend docs: true means 'a successful basic check of structures' and 'this is not a sign of successful execution of a trade operation'; 'we should first check the retcode'. MqlTradeRequest docs: Instant/Request require action, symbol, volume, price, sl, tp, deviation, type, type_filling; Market/Exchange require only action, symbol, volume, type, type_filling. MT5 help: Instant Execution sends a 'Requote' if the price is rejected; in Market Execution the broker decides the price 'without any additional discussion with a trader' and sending the order 'means advance consent'. The 'slippage is not a protection' part was labelled an inference in the report, but I found it stated outright in the official MQL5 Book: 'The deviation field affects the execution of market orders only in the Instant Execution and Request Execution modes.' fact_check.claim: The built-in MQL5 economic calendar works only in a live, connected terminal: in the Strategy Tester calendar calls fail (error 4014 FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED) or return nothing, and calendar timestamps are in trade-server time, with historical events mis-shifted by an hour for the part of the year when DST state differs.
fact_check.note: Tried to refute by looking for a newer build that added calendar history to the tester; found none. Official MQL5 Book: 'Calendar functions cannot be used in the tester', error FUNCTION_NOT_ALLOWED (4014), and the developer 'must independently change the times of historical news in those periods' when DST mode differs. MQL5 reference: 'All functions for working with the economic calendar use the trade server time.' MQL5 article 22580 (28 May 2026): 'None work in the Strategy Tester because the tester has no server connection during historical replay', with a CSV export workaround. I read the official MetaTrader 5 release notes for every listed build from March 2025 through Build 6230 (24 September 2026, the newest listed): no entry mentions calendar support in the Strategy Tester; the only calendar item is the AI Assistant reading the calendar in Build 6230. The forum thread the report flagged as possibly contradicting (449652) does not: a moderator there states 'Calendar data is not available in Backtest. Only live you can request data', and the 'it works' reply only links a workaround video. Caveats: the limitation is stated in the Book and articles, not on the reference page for testing itself; and absence from release notes is not proof, so a one-line runtime check in the tester is still worthwhile. Search budget exhausted; verification was by direct fetch of primary pages.

fact_check.claim: Broker server time is typically GMT+2 in winter and GMT+3 in US summer time (New York-close alignment), switching on US DST dates; MQL5 offers no reliable server-UTC offset, and TimeGMT() depends on the local PC clock. Session filters built on fixed hour offsets drift by one hour during the US/EU DST mismatch weeks.
fact_check.note: Platform facts confirmed on primary pages; the 'typically' is a generalisation from only two brokers. CONFIRMED: IC Markets sheet: 'To align the daily chart candles with New York close (5pm ET) IC Markets server time and charts are GMT + 2 or GMT + 3 when daylight savings is in effect' (it does not say which country's DST). Pepperstone: 'Server time is set to GMT +3 while US daylight savings is in place' and GMT+2 otherwise. MQL5 docs: TimeGMT() is 'calculated taking into account the DST switch by the local time' on the computer, and 'During testing in the strategy tester, TimeGMT() is always equal to TimeTradeServer() simulated server time'; TimeTradeServer() is calculated 'in the client terminal and depends on the time settings on your computer'; the testing page says local, server and GMT time are all equal in the tester, deliberately. So a server-UTC offset computed in the tester is always zero: a hard constraint for backtesting session and news filters. FTMO update of 12 Mar 2026 confirms platform time GMT+3, Max Daily Loss monitored in Prague time, and that from 29 Mar 2026 the offset 'will again be just 1 hour'. Caveats: (1) the cited FTMO page does not contain the '8 Mar 2026' date; that is simply the US DST start date, so the 2-hour-offset window is inferred, not quoted; (2) 'no reliable server-UTC offset' is an inference: live, TimeTradeServer() minus TimeGMT() works if the PC clock is correct, it only fails in the tester; (3) GMT+2/+3 with US DST is common but not universal, so the bot must measure the offset on the actual broker rather than assume it. Search budget exhausted, so I could not search for brokers using other conventions.

fact_check.claim: Prop-firm rule sets differ by firm, by programme and over time; the bot needs a configurable compliance layer (daily loss anchored to the firm's clock, static vs end-of-day vs intraday trailing max loss, news execution windows that also cover SL/TP fills, best-day consistency caps, order-count limits).
fact_check.note: Numbers re-checked on the firms' own pages (fetched 2026-11-14). FTMO objectives: 2-Step daily loss 5% of initial capital measured from the balance at 00:00 CE(S)T, tested on equity ('Balance + Open Positions P/L ± Swaps – Commissions'); Max Loss 10% static; targets 10% then 5%; minimum 4 trading days. 1-Step: daily loss 3%, Max Loss 10% end-of-day trailing. Instant: daily loss 3%, 10% intraday balance-based trailing, best day <= 30% of total profit. All match the report. One wording correction: for orders from 12 Oct 2026 the 1-Step rule is called 'Consistency' and 'replaces the Best Day Rule' (best day <= 50% of total profit); the legacy Best Day Rule (orders before that date) is 50% of Positive Days' Profit, a different denominator. Both are 'not treated as a rule breach'. This rule change itself confirms the 'over time' part. FTMO news FAQ: execution restricted '2 minutes before and 2 minutes after', 'including your Stop Loss, Take Profit or any other pending orders'; Swing and Challenge/Verification exempt; Gold (XAUUSD) listed for USD events, XAGUSD not listed; violation 'may result in termination'. FTMO strategies FAQ: 'a limit of 200 orders at a time' and '2000 max positions per day' confirmed; the 'maximum capital allocation rule' is named but not defined. The5ers: High Stakes 2 minutes before/after, judged at trigger time, profits deducted, bracketing banned elsewhere: confirmed. FundedNext: 5 minutes before/after, 40% of profit counted, on Stellar 1-Step, 2-Step and Lite funded accounts, including SL/TP and pending orders: confirmed. NOT VERIFIED: the FundingPips figures (5 or 10 minute windows, 5-hour exemption, 35%/15% consistency) because its help centre returned HTTP 403; treat those numbers as unconfirmed. Search budget exhausted; no independent search for later rule changes was possible.
